# Output Interpretation



AlphaFold produces a rich, multi-layered output directory for each prediction target. Understanding what each file contains, how confidence metrics are computed, and how to read the structural representations is essential for extracting biological insight from raw predictions. This page decodes every output artifact, explains the confidence scoring system, and maps the logic by which models are ranked and selected.

## Output Directory Structure

When AlphaFold completes a prediction for a target (e.g., `my_protein`), it writes results into `<output_dir>/my_protein/`. The following diagram illustrates the complete output tree and the data flow that produces each artifact:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ModelInference["Model Inference (×5 models)"]
        A[Processed Features] --> B[Neural Network Forward Pass]
        B --> C[Prediction Result Dict]
    end

    subgraph ConfidenceMetrics["Confidence Computation"]
        C --> D[pLDDT per residue]
        C --> E[PAE matrix]
        C --> F[pTM score]
        C --> G[ipTM score]
        D --> H[ranking_confidence]
        F --> H
        G --> H
    end

    subgraph StructureOutput["Structure Output"]
        C --> I[Protein Object]
        D --> J[B-factors = pLDDT]
        I --> J
        J --> K[unrelaxed PDB]
        J --> L[unrelaxed mmCIF]
    end

    subgraph Relaxation["Amber Relaxation"]
        K --> M[Relaxed PDB]
        K --> N[Relaxed mmCIF]
        M --> O[Relax Metrics JSON]
    end

    subgraph Ranking["Model Ranking"]
        H --> P[ranking_debug.json]
        P --> Q[ranked_0.pdb ... ranked_4.pdb]
    end

    C --> R[result_model_X.pkl]
    D --> S[confidence_model_X.json]
    E --> T[pae_model_X.json]
```

The table below enumerates every output file, its format, and the scope of its content:

| File Pattern | Format | Scope | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `features.pkl` | Pickle dict | Per target | Input feature dictionary fed to all models |
| `result_model_{1..5}.pkl` | Pickle dict | Per model | Full prediction result including logits, structure module outputs, and confidence metrics |
| `confidence_model_{1..5}.json` | JSON | Per model | Per-residue pLDDT scores and confidence categories |
| `pae_model_{1..5}.json` | JSON | Per model | Predicted Aligned Error matrix (monomer_ptm and multimer only) |
| `unrelaxed_model_{1..5}.pdb` | PDB | Per model | Predicted structure before Amber relaxation, pLDDT in B-factor column |
| `unrelaxed_model_{1..5}.cif` | mmCIF | Per model | Same structure in mmCIF format |
| `relaxed_model_{1..5}.pdb` | PDB | Per model | Amber-relaxed structure (only if relaxation enabled for this model) |
| `relaxed_model_{1..5}.cif` | mmCIF | Per model | Relaxed structure in mmCIF format |
| `ranked_{0..4}.pdb` | PDB | Per rank | Structures sorted by ranking confidence (rank 0 = best) |
| `ranked_{0..4}.cif` | mmCIF | Per rank | Ranked structures in mmCIF format |
| `ranking_debug.json` | JSON | Per target | Model ranking scores and sorted order |
| `timings.json` | JSON | Per target | Wall-clock time for each pipeline stage |
| `relax_metrics.json` | JSON | Per target | Amber relaxation violations and energy metrics |
| `msas/` | Directory | Per target | Intermediate MSA files (if not using precomputed MSAs) |

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L345-L556), [run_alphold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L288-L343)

## Confidence Metrics Deep Dive

AlphaFold's confidence system is the primary mechanism for assessing prediction quality. Three interrelated metrics operate at different granularities: **pLDDT** scores individual residues, **pTM** scores the entire structure globally, and **PAE** captures pairwise positional uncertainty between residue pairs.

### pLDDT — Per-Residue Confidence

The **predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT)** estimates how close the predicted structure's local distance matrix is to the true structure, on a per-residue basis. It is computed from the `PredictedLDDTHead` logits via a softmax over bins, then an expectation over bin centers:

```
bin_width = 1.0 / num_bins
bin_centers = [0.5 × bin_width, 1.5 × bin_width, ..., (num_bins - 0.5) × bin_width]
probs = softmax(logits, axis=-1)
pLDDT = 100 × Σ(prob_i × bin_center_i)
```

The result is a `[num_res]` array with values in **[0, 100]**. AlphaFold categorizes each residue into four quality bands:

| Score Range | Category | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 0 – 49 | **D** (Disordered) | Very low confidence; residue is likely unstructured or intrinsically disordered |
| 50 – 69 | **L** (Low) | Low confidence; backbone may be approximately correct but side chains unreliable |
| 70 – 89 | **M** (Medium) | Generally reliable backbone prediction; some side-chain uncertainty |
| 90 – 100 | **H** (High) | High confidence; both backbone and side chain likely correct |

> [!TIP]
> The pLDDT values are written directly into the **B-factor column** of every output PDB file. This means you can color structures by confidence in any molecular viewer (e.g., PyMOL, ChimeraX) by coloring by B-factor — the standard AlphaFold visualization uses the D/L/M/H color scheme (orange/yellow/cyan/blue).

Sources: [confidence.py](/alphafold/common/confidence.py#L30-L58), [confidence.py](/alphafold/common/confidence.py#L61-L81), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L447-L456)

### pTM — Predicted TM-Score

The **predicted Template Modeling score (pTM)** provides a single scalar assessing the overall fold correctness of the predicted structure relative to the (unknown) true structure. It is derived from the `PredictedAlignedErrorHead` logits:

```
d0 = 1.24 × (clipped_num_res - 15)^(1/3) - 1.8
tm_per_bin = 1 / (1 + (bin_center / d0)²)
predicted_tm_term = Σ(prob_i × tm_per_bin_i)
pTM = max_alignment(Σ(predicted_tm_term × normed_residue_weights))
```

The `d0` constant follows the standard TM-score definition from Yang & Skolnick (2004). Values range from 0 to 1, where **pTM > 0.5** generally suggests the predicted overall fold is correct, and **pTM < 0.5** suggests the fold may be incorrect or the protein may not adopt a single stable conformation.

Sources: [confidence.py](/alphafold/common/confidence.py#L184-L244)

### ipTM — Interface Predicted TM-Score

For **multimer** predictions only, AlphaFold additionally computes the **interface pTM (ipTM)**, which restricts the TM-score computation to **residue pairs across different chains** (i.e., where `asym_id[i] ≠ asym_id[j]`). This isolates the confidence assessment to the inter-chain interface — the biologically critical region for complexes.

Sources: [model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L51-L58)

### PAE — Predicted Aligned Error

The **Predicted Aligned Error (PAE)** is a `[num_res × num_res]` matrix where entry `(i, j)` estimates the expected positional error (in Ångströms) of residue `j` when the predicted structure is superimposed onto the true structure at residue `i`. Computation:

```
bin_centers = breaks + step/2  (with catch-all final bin)
PAE[i,j] = Σ(aligned_distance_error_probs[i,j,k] × bin_center_k)
```

**How to read PAE**: A block-diagonal pattern with low values within blocks and high values between blocks indicates well. A uniform or noisy PAE suggests.? A **low PAE; a) between two domains indicates confidence in their relative placement+'s relative orientation. The `max_predicted2` value3` defines` the` upper bound of the error` scale` (typically ~31.75 Å).

Sources: [confidence.py](/alphafold/common/confidence.py#L102-L155), [confidence.py](/alphaf4d>old/common/confidence.py#L158-L181)

## Model Ranking Logic

AlphaFold runs1 runs 5 distinct model parameters (model_1 through model_5), each producing a complete prediction. The models are **ranked by( by by** `ranking_confidence`, which is computed differently for monomer and multimer modes:

| Mode | Ranking Formula |G | Rationale |
|---|---|---E|
| **Monomer** (`monomer`, `monomer_casp14`, `monomer_ptm`) | `mean(pLDDT)` | Average per-residue confidence across all residues |
| **Multimer**C | `B `0.8 × ipTMG + 0.2G ×5 × pTM` | Heavily weights interface quality while retaining global fold assessment |

The ranked order is written to `ranking_debug.json` along with the raw scores. The key within this JSON is either `"plddts' "`` plddts` " (monomer) or `''iptm+ptm''` `` iptm+ptm` ` (multimer), reflecting the ranking metric used.

Sources: [model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L31-L69), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L473-L545)

## The result.pkl Dictionary

Each `result_model_{n}.pkl` contains the full, unprocessed prediction dictionary. This is the most detailed output and includes the following major keys:

| Key | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `structure_module.final_atom_positions` | `[num_res, 37, 3]` | All-atom coordinates (37 atom types per residue) |
| `structure_module.final_atom_mask` | `[num_res, 37]` | Binary mask for which atoms are present |
| `structure_module.sidechain_frames` | `[num_res, 8, 3]` | Rigid body frames for side chain atoms |
| `structure_module.sidechain_atom_pos` | `[num_res, 14, 3]` | Side chain atom positions |
| `predicted_lddt.logits` | `[num_res, num_bins]` | Raw logits from PredictedLDDTHead |
| `predicted_aligned_error.logits` | `[num_res, num_res, num_bins]` | Raw logits from PredictedAlignedErrorHead |
| `predicted_aligned_error.breaks` | `[num_bins - 1]` | Bin edge definitions for PAE |
| `plddt` | `[num_res]` | Computed pLDDT scores (0–100) |
| `predicted_aligned_error` | `[num_res, num_res]` | Computed PAE matrix (Å) |
| `max_predicted_aligned_error` | scalar | Maximum PAE value possible |
| `ptm` | scalar | Predicted TM-score |
| `iptm` | scalar | Interface pTM (multimer only) |
| `ranking_confidence` | scalar | Score used for model ranking |

Sources: [model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L31-L69), [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L343-L381)

## Protein Data Representation in Output Files

The `Protein` dataclass is the canonical internal representation that bridges the neural network output and the serialized PDB/mmCIF files. Its six fields capture the complete structural state:

| Field | Shape | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `atom_positions` | `[num_res, 37, 3]` | Cartesian coordinates in Å (N, CA, CB, ... order) |
| `aatype` | `[num_res]` | Amino acid integer (0–20, where 20 = unknown) |
| `atom_mask` | `[num_res, 37]` | 1.0 if atom present, 0.0 otherwise |
| `residue_index` | `[num_res]` | PDB residue number (not necessarily 0-indexed or contiguous) |
| `chain_index` | `[num_res]` | 0-indexed chain identifier |
| `b_factors` | `[num_res, 37]` | B-factors; **set to pLDDT** in AlphaFold outputs |

> [!TIP]
> When reading AlphaFold P9 PDB output6 in downstream tools, the B-factor column contains pLDDT scores (repeated across all atoms within a residue), **not** experimental B-factors. This is an intentional design choice — it enables immediate confidence visualization. If you need true crystallographic B-factors, you must supply them separately.

The conversion from model output to `Protein` object via `from_prediction()` extracts `final_atom_positions` and `final_atom_mask` from the `structure_module` output, maps `asym_id` features to `chain_index` (multimer) or defaults to zero (monomer), and injects pLDDT as B-factors. The PDB serialization then writes each atom in strict PDB columnar format (80-character lines), while the mmCIF serialization produces a standards-compliant mmCIF with `_entity_poly_seq`, `_struct_asym`, `_chem_comp`, and `_atom_site` tables.

Sources: [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L64-L97), [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L343-L381), [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L232-L324), [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L384-L:520)

## Amber Relaxation Outputs

When enabled (via `--models_to_relax=best` or `all`), Amber relaxation performs energy minimization on the predicted structure to resolve stereochemical violations (clashing atoms, unrealistic bond lengths/angles). The relaxation process yields:

1. **Relaxed PDB/mmCIF** — the energy-minimized structure, with original pLDDT B-factors preserved via `overwrite_b_factors()`
2. **`relax_metrics.json`** — per-model dictionary containing:
   - `remaining_violations` — boolean list of per-residue violation flags after relaxation
   - `remaining_violations_count` — total number of residues still violating after relaxation

The `AmberRelaxation.process()` method additionally computes internal debug data (initial energy, final energy, RMSD between pre- and post-relaxation positions, number of minimization attempts), though these are logged rather than persisted to disk.

The `--models_to_relax` flag controls scope: `BEST` relaxes only the top-ranked model, `ALL` relaxes every model, and `NONE` skips relaxation entirely (useful if relaxation causes issues). After relaxation, the `ranked_{0..4}.pdb` files prefer the relaxed version when available, falling back to the unrelaxed PDB.

Sources: [relax.py](/alphafold/relax/relax.py#L23-L90), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L481-L536)

## Interpreting Multimer vs. Monomer Outputs

The output structure differs subtly between prediction modes:

| Aspect | Monomer | Multimer |
|---|---|---|
| PAE JSON files | Only with `monomer_ptm` preset | Always present |
| ipTM value | Not computed | Computed and stored in result.pkl |
| `ranking_debug.json` key | `"plddts"` | `"iptm+ptm"` |
| `chain_index` | All zeros (single chain) | Mapped from `asym_id` feature |
| Predictions per model | 1 | `" × `num_multimer_predictions_per_model` (default 5), yielding up to 25 total predictions |
| mmCIF `_entity_poly` | Single entity | Multiple entities, one per unique chain |

For multimer predictions, the increased prediction count (5 models × 5 seeds = 25 predictions) means the output directory will contain correspondingly more `result_*.pkl`, `confidence_*.json`, and `p9ae_*.json` files, all ranked into the same `ranked_{0..N}.pdb` sequence.

Sources: [model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L51-L61), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L538-L545)

## Quick Interpretation Checklist

When evaluating an AlphaFold prediction, follow this decision sequence:

1. **Check `ranking_debug.json`** — identify the best model and its ranking confidence score
2. **Inspect `ranked_0.pdb` B-factors** — color by confidence; residues below pLDDT 50 are likely disordered
3. **Read `pae_model_*.json`** — look for block-diagonal patterns indicating domain organization and inter-domain confidence
4. **Assess pTM/ipTM** — pTM > 0.5 suggests correct global fold; for multimers, ipTM > 0.8 indicates reliable interface
5. **Review `relax_metrics.json`** — high violation counts may indicate stereochemical issues even after relaxation
6. **Compare across models** — consistent predictions across the 5 models increase confidence in the result

For deeper understanding of the confidence algorithms, see [pLDDT and pTM Scoring](17-plddt-and-ptm-scoring) and [Predicted Aligned Error](18-predicted-aligned-error). For the protein data representation details, see [Protein Data Representation](20-protein-data-representation). For relaxation mechanics, see [Amber Relaxation](19-amber-relaxation).


# Latest Updates



The AlphaFold 2 repository has been undergoing a quiet but consequential modernization campaign. While the broader AlphaFold ecosystem — the database, the server, the Nobel halo — grabs headlines, the open-source codebase has been getting its plumbing overhauled. Meanwhile, the institutional landscape around the project has shifted dramatically. Here is what matters.

## The Codebase Modernization Push (Oct 2025 – Apr 2026)

The last six months of commits tell a clear story: the AlphaFold 2 repo is being cleaned up for long-term maintainability. This is not feature work — it is the unglamorous but essential work of removing technical debt that accumulates in any project sitting at the intersection of three fast-moving ecosystems (Python, JAX, CUDA).

### Dependency Diet: scipy Eliminated Entirely

The single most significant arc in recent commits is the **complete removal of scipy as a dependency**, executed by Harsh Tiku across four commits in October 2025:

1. [Replace `scipy.linalg.block_diag` with a NumPy implementation](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a2581aef159492e296c16cedd33eb711f6d323e5) — Oct 24
2. [Replace custom `block_diagonal` with `jax.scipy.linalg.block_diag`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a138beeaf1c4c6052d33e6467049aa2fe181757b) — Oct 27
3. [Migrate `softmax` calls from `scipy` to `jax.scipy`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/78a01da677c4d7705a7a8083486615d7c3c3252b) — Oct 27
4. [Use custom `ks_normal_test` to approximate normality testing](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/d172b1a6c7df686e3a9766fe39d443880c41ae3b) — Oct 30
5. [Remove last traces of scipy](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/40be3ec6c764fd7e8f4478ac6280f438058e271a) — Oct 31

This is a meaningful simplification. scipy is a heavy dependency — it pulls in compiled Fortran/C code via numpy and has historically been a source of build headaches in containerized and HPC environments. Replacing it with pure NumPy and `jax.scipy` equivalents reduces the installation surface area and aligns the codebase more tightly with JAX as the sole computational backend.

However, one choice deserves scrutiny: the custom `ks_normal_test` that approximates the Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value is an *approximation*, not an exact replacement. For production structure prediction this is unlikely to matter (the normality test feeds into confidence estimation, not the core folding), but anyone forking AlphaFold for statistical research should be aware of the substitution.

### Packaging: setup.py → pyproject.toml

[Augustin Zidek migrated the project from `setup.py` to `pyproject.toml`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/cd0357af72396da3b75fe4c9cf86f8d9ba4e4d4e) on October 24, 2025 — a move that brings AlphaFold in line with [PEP 621](https://peps.python.org/pep-0621/) and modern Python packaging conventions. This also resolved [a community request](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1099) asking for the formatting configuration used in the recent `pyformat` reformatting, which was later addressed by [adding pyink configuration to pyproject.toml](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/59cbb686da5a5cf1764a347f7332d7026c1b65fb).

For anyone maintaining a fork, this is a breaking change in terms of merge conflicts — but the `pyproject.toml` migration is a one-time pain that makes future tooling integration (linting, type checking, build systems) significantly cleaner.

### OpenMM and PDBfixer: Conda No More

[OpenMM and PDBfixer were previously installed via Conda](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a4315dd7b8f9f543ad5f4080af4a42d431ef3b35); as of March 10, 2026, both are now on PyPI and installed via pip. OpenMM was simultaneously bumped from 8.0.0 to 8.2.0 for PyPI compatibility. This is another simplification that eliminates Conda as a build dependency — a long-standing pain point documented in [community guides about Conda-Pack and OpenMM](https://www.blopig.com/blog/2023/07/the-dangers-of-conda-pack-and-openmm) that warned about environment portability issues with OpenMM's compiled extensions.

### Compatibility and Cleanup

The remaining commits form a consistent cleanup narrative:

| Date | Commit | Significance |
|------|--------|-------------|
| Feb 3, 2026 | [Fix Numpy 2.4 compatibility](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/dc61fb4a31bd15c4b3363281217e125d34748892) | Unblocks users on latest NumPy |
| Mar 3, 2026 | [Inline softmax for old JAX compatibility](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/636a18bae7137ffe7b4d946f1be12e25adc877fc) | Prevents breakage on pinned JAX |
| Apr 2, 2026 | [Remove unsupported Python versions](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafock/commit/4593e8c4118b12ae2260a268a18a42deb7569a31) | Drops EOL Pythons |
| Apr 7, 2026 | [Use `gcloud storage` instead of `gsutil`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/27fb0c0b898af876f2801168ab22899d043389f5) | Aligns with current GCloud CLI |
| Apr 13–14, 2026 | [Remove dead TF transform code](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/7e1e321dfd7f9df5c8cf17b3f2a64fc794d18b1a) | Prunes legacy TensorFlow paths |

The NumPy 2.4 fix and the JAX softmax inlining are particularly telling — they signal that the maintainers are actively tracking upstream breakage in the scientific Python stack rather than pinning to stale versions. This is the right approach for a project that is widely deployed across heterogeneous HPC environments, even if it means more frequent compatibility patches.

```mermaid
timeline
    title AlphaFold 2 Codebase Modernization Timeline
    section 2025 Q4
        Oct 24 : pyproject.toml migration
        Oct 24-31 : scipy removal (5 commits)
        Oct 16 : layer_norm epsilon constant
    section 2026 Q1
        Jan 9 : pyink config added
        Feb 3 : NumPy 2.4 compat fix
        Mar 3 : Inline softmax (JAX compat)
        Mar 10 : OpenMM/PDBfixer → PyPI
        Mar 12 : Distillation set note update
    section 2026 Q2
        Apr 2 : Drop EOL Python versions
        Apr 7 : gsutil → gcloud storage
        Apr 13-14 : Remove dead TF transforms
        Apr 22 : AFS custom template JSON update
```

## AlphaFold Database: Partnership Renewed, Complexes Released

While the codebase changes are incremental, the AlphaFold Database (AFDB) has seen major updates on the data side.

### EMBL-EBI Partnership Renewal (March 2026)

[EMBL-EBI and Google DeepMind renewed their collaboration](https://www.embl.org/news/science-technology/google-deepmind-partnership-renewal) on the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The renewal came with significant data updates:

- **UniProt 2025_03 sync**: The database now covers newly discovered proteins.
- **Protein isoforms**: For the first time, AFDB includes isoforms — functionally distinct variants of the same protein. This is valuable for tissue-specific and disease-associated analyses.
- **MSAs available for download**: The multiple sequence alignments used to generate predictions are now downloadable, opening a new layer of evolutionary and structural analysis.

The AFDB update was described in a [Nucleic Acids Research paper](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41273079) (Bertoni et al., 2026), which also documents a comprehensive redesign of the entry page with integrated 3D viewers, domain tabs, and annotation overlays.

### Protein Complexes Release (May 2026)

In May 2026, a collaboration between EMBL-EBI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, and Seoul National University released **~2.2 million homodimeric and ~79,000 heterodimeric high-confidence protein complex structures** into AFDB. This covers ~19M homomeric and ~8M heteromeric predictions across 4,777 proteomes, including 16 model organisms and 30 WHO-prioritized proteomes. The full set of ~31 million predictions is available for bulk download. This directly addresses the long-standing community interest in multimer prediction that [issue #269](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/269) (now closed) once requested.

## The Team Folds: Jumper Leaves for Anthropic

The most significant organizational development is the dissolution of the dedicated AlphaFold team at Google DeepMind.

On June 19, 2026, [John Jumper announced he was leaving DeepMind for Anthropic](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/19/john-jumper-to-leave-google-deepmind-for-anthropic.html), after nearly nine years. Jumper was the lead architect of AlphaFold 2 and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Demis Hassabis for the work. As [reported by Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-google-deepmind-broke-up-the-alphafold-team), some team members left the company, others were reassigned within Google, and some moved to Isomorphic Labs. A DeepMind spokesperson confirmed many of these moves happened more than a year ago.

Jumper's departure is symbolically weighty but practically nuanced. As CASP co-founder John Moult put it: *"They did it. What's the next mission?"* The AlphaFold code is open source, the database is maintained by EMBL-EBI, and independent groups (ColabFold, OpenFold, Boltz) have already reproduced and extended the core predictions. The team's dissolution is unlikely to slow the field.

However, the departure does raise questions about the maintenance trajectory of the `google-deepmind/alphafold` repository itself. The recent commits are almost entirely from Augustin Zidek and Harsh Tiku, suggesting that a small team is keeping the lights on. Whether this maintenance continues at the current pace — or whether the community picks up the slack via forks — remains to be seen.

## Hardware Frontier: Blackwell GPU Compatibility

The open [RTX PRO 6000 / SM_120 incompatibility issue](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1121) highlights a growing pain: NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture (compute capability SM_120) is not yet cleanly supported by the JAX/XLA stack that AlphaFold depends on. The issue author reports trying "a dozen possible combinations between jax, cuda, haiku, etc." with XLA failing to initialize CUDA.

This is not an AlphaFold-specific problem — it is a JAX ecosystem issue — but it is a reminder that AlphaFold's hardware compatibility is entirely downstream of JAX's. Users planning GPU purchases (as in [issue #1125](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1125) about workstation GPU selection) should verify JAX + CUDA compatibility for their target card before committing, rather than assuming that "NVIDIA GPU" is sufficient.

## What to Watch

1. **Repository maintenance cadence**: Will commits continue at the current ~2-4/month rate post-team-dissolution, or will it slow further? The [AFDB README update to `gcloud storage`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/27fb0c0b898af876f2801168ab22899d043389f5) suggests at least one maintainer is still actively tracking external tooling changes.
2. **JAX + Blackwell**: Once JAX lands SM_120 support, AlphaFold should work on Blackwell without code changes. Track the [JAX GPU support matrix](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax) for updates.
3. **Community forks**: With the core team dispersed, community-driven forks like [OpenFold](https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold) may become the more actively developed path for structural biologists who need modifications beyond what the official repo provides.
4. **AFDB complex data**: The ~31M complex predictions now available for bulk download will likely trigger a wave of functional annotation and interaction studies. The [bulk MSA download question](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1111) remains open — rate limits for programmatic access are still undocumented.

The codebase is cleaner than it has been in years. The institutional scaffolding around it is thinner than it has been in years. Both things are true at the same time, and both matter for anyone building on AlphaFold in production.

# Issues and Feedbacks



The AlphaFold 2 issue tracker is a fascinating document in its own right. With 276 open issues and a repository that sits at 14.8k stars, it captures the collision between a research-grade codebase and a production-hungry scientific community. The pattern is consistent: DeepMind ships a breakthrough, the world tries to deploy it on every conceivable hardware and workflow, and the friction points that emerge reveal structural gaps in how scientific software gets maintained after the paper is published.

What follows is a categorised tour of the most persistent and representative issues -- the ones that keep coming back, the ones that reveal real architectural limitations, and the ones where the community has stepped in with workarounds that deserve wider attention.

---

## The Long Tail of Deployment Pain

### HHSearch Silently Fails on HPC Clusters

[Issue #897](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/897) -- opened February 2024, still open as of May 2026 -- is a masterclass in how hard it is to debug a silent failure in a containerised pipeline. The symptom is maddeningly terse:

```
RuntimeError: HHSearch failed:
stdout:

stderr:
```

No output at all. HHSearch runs, exits, and takes its reasoning with it. The reporter is using a Singularity image on a Slurm-managed cluster with 64 GB of memory -- well above the typical requirement -- and has tried the `-DHAVE_AVX2=1` compilation flag suggested in [hh-suite issue #282](https://github.com/soedinglab/hh-suite/issues/282) without success.

This is not an isolated case. The same error pattern appears in [ColabFold issue #575](https://github.com/sokrypton/ColabFold/issues/575), where the underlying cause turns out to be corrupted or empty `pdb70_cs219.ffindex` files. The [University of Illinois IGB cluster documentation](https://help.igb.illinois.edu/Biocluster_Alphafold) explicitly calls out this error and recommends increasing memory allocation as the first fix, which suggests the root cause is often a resource issue during the database build or copy step that silently produces truncated index files.

**The structural problem:** AlphaFold's Docker image bundles HHSearch as a pre-compiled binary against specific CPU instruction sets and database formats. When the database files are corrupted -- often due to incomplete downloads, filesystem permission issues, or memory pressure during extraction -- HHSearch fails silently. There is no pre-flight validation of the databases, no checksum verification, and no meaningful error message. For a pipeline where the MSA/template search is a prerequisite for everything that follows, this is a brittle design.

### Out of Memory: A Recurring Classic

[Issue #392](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/392) documents the GPU out-of-memory error that has haunted AlphaFold since its initial release. The traceback shows XLA trying to allocate **30.46 GiB** in a single shot:

```
Allocator (GPU_0_bfc) ran out of memory trying to allocate 30.46GiB
```

This was supposedly fixed in v2.1.2 by addressing CUDA/jaxlib version incompatibilities, but the issue keeps reappearing with new GPU generations and driver versions. The [UCSF AlphaFold performance page](https://www.rbvi.ucsf.edu/chimerax/data/alphafold-jan2022/afspeed.html) documents concrete limits: a 24 GB RTX 3090 fails on proteins above ~2,500 amino acids with `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`, while a 48 GB A40 can handle structures up to ~3,800 amino acids.

The practical guidance that has emerged from the community:

| GPU VRAM | Approx. Max Sequence Length | Typical Time (500 aa) |
|----------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| 16 GB (T4/P100) | ~1,000 aa | 5-10 min |
| 24 GB (3090/4090) | ~2,000 aa | 1-5 min |
| 48 GB (A40/A6000) | ~3,800 aa | 0.5-2 min |

---

## Next-Generation Hardware: The Blackwell Wall

### SM_120 Incompatibility

[Issue #1121](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1121) is the most consequential open issue for anyone investing in current-generation hardware. The question is simple: can AlphaFold 2 run on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (RTX PRO 6000, RTX PRO 4500)? The answer, right now, is **no**.

The core error, as documented by commenter `k127soo`:

```
jaxlib.xla_extension.XlaRuntimeError: INTERNAL:
ptxas exited with non-zero error code 65280, output:
ptxas fatal: Program with .target 'sm_90a' cannot be compiled to future architecture
```

The problem is architectural. The JAX/XLA stack inside AlphaFold 2's Docker container generates PTX code targeting `sm_90a` (Ada Lovelace / Hopper). Blackwell's compute capability 12.0 (`sm_120`) is a "future architecture" from the perspective of this PTX, and NVIDIA's `ptxas` compiler refuses to forward-compile it. This is not an AlphaFold-specific problem -- the same `cudaErrorNoKernelImageForDevice` error appears across the ecosystem, as documented in [this Cellpose forum thread](https://forum.image.sc/t/cellpose-with-nvidia-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell-problem/119144) and [vLLM discussion boards](https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/support-for-rtx-6000-blackwell-96gb-card/1707).

The fix requires rebuilding the entire JAX/jaxlib/XLA toolchain with Blackwell-compatible CUDA (12.8+), and potentially updating Haiku and every other JAX-dependent library in the dependency graph. As commenter `Russ-Peter` notes, [issue #1085](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1085) (which addresses consumer RTX 5090 cards) doesn't help with the professional Blackwell line.

**This is a maintenance gap that will only widen.** Blackwell GPUs are shipping now. Research groups buying new workstations will hit this wall immediately. The absence of an official Dockerfile update or requirements.txt that works on SM_120 is a real deployment blocker.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[NVIDIA Blackwell GPU<br/>sm_120 / CC 12.0] --> B[JAX/XLA in AF2 Container]
    B --> C[PTX targets sm_90a]
    C --> D{ptxas compilation}
    D -->|sm_90a → sm_120| E[❌ Fatal: cannot compile<br/>to future architecture]
    D -->|sm_90a → sm_90a| F[✅ Works on Ada/Hopper]
    E --> G[Required: Rebuild JAX stack<br/>with CUDA 12.8+ and sm_120 target]
```

---

## Infrastructure and Orchestration Friction

### GPU Slowdown on Kubernetes

[Issue #1094](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1094) reports a 3x slowdown in GPU inference time when running AlphaFold 2 on Kubernetes compared to bare Docker on the same host shape. CPU-bound MSA generation time is identical -- only the GPU phase is affected. The reporter confirms there are no IOPS issues since all data runs from hostpath.

This is a known class of problem with GPU passthrough in containerised environments. Common causes include:

- **GPU device plugin overhead** in Kubernetes (NVIDIA device plugin vs. native Docker `--gpus`)
- **Memory mapping / NUMA affinity** loss when the GPU is not pinned to the correct NUMA node
- **CUDA context setup latency** repeated per pod invocation vs. persistent Docker container
- **Missing `--shm-size`** configuration in the pod spec (Kubernetes defaults to 64 MB; AlphaFold needs significantly more shared memory for XLA)

The issue has no resolution yet, which points to a broader problem: AlphaFold's deployment documentation is Docker-centric, and Kubernetes orchestration requires non-obvious pod spec tuning that most researchers discover through painful iteration.

### Best GPU for Local AlphaFold

[Issue #1125](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1125) asks the practical question: what GPU should you buy for a local workstation running ~10,000 predictions of 750-1,500 aa proteins? The candidates are RTX 4090 (24 GB), RTX 5090 (~32 GB), and RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB).

Based on the [deploybase.ai GPU comparison for protein folding](https://deploybase.ai/articles/best-gpu-cloud-for-protein-folding-provider-pricing-comparison) and community benchmarks, the answer depends critically on sequence length:

- **RTX 4090 (24 GB):** Handles sequences up to ~2,000 aa. For 750-1,500 aa proteins, this is sufficient and cost-effective (~$1,500). Prediction time: ~5-10 min per protein.
- **RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB):** Needed for sequences approaching 3,000+ aa. At ~$6,800, it's 4.5x the price for 2x the VRAM. Worth it only if you regularly hit OOM on 24 GB cards.
- **Multiple 4090s vs. single 6000:** AlphaFold 2 inference runs on a single GPU. Multiple GPUs benefit only through parallel batch processing of independent sequences. For throughput, two 4090s (~$3,000) outperform one 6000 Ada for most workloads.

**The RTX 5090 is the wildcard.** If it delivers ~32 GB VRAM at consumer pricing, it could become the sweet spot for AlphaFold 2 -- but it faces the same Blackwell SM_120 incompatibility as the professional cards until the JAX stack is updated.

---

## Data Access: The MSA Bulk Download Gap

[Issue #1111](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1111) exposes a significant gap in the AlphaFold Database infrastructure. The user needs to download MSA files for **several million proteins**, and none of the documented channels work at scale:

| Channel | Limitation |
|---------|------------|
| Individual API downloads (`alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/files/msa/`) | No documented rate limits; works per-file but uncertain at millions of requests |
| [Google Cloud public bucket](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/bigquery-public-data/deepmind-alphafold) | Limited to v4; **does not include MSA files** |
| [EBI FTP server](https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/alphafold/) | Changelog mentions MSA updates, but actual MSA files are not found in the directory structure |

The [EBI training documentation](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/navigating-alphafold-database/what-is-the-afdb/accessing-searching-afdb/bulk-downloads-ftp) confirms that the FTP server provides bulk PDB/mmCIF downloads for proteomes and mentions that MSAs are available in `msas` subdirectories within collaboration chunks, but there is no documented mechanism for bulk MSA access by UniProt ID.

Community commenter `NishikaGolani` offers an AWS-specific workaround: pre-stage MSA databases on **FSx for Lustre**, so the first job pays the cold I/O cost and subsequent jobs hit cached pages. This reportedly delivers 10-15x faster startup. But this only works if you can get the data in the first place -- and the question of how to avoid EBI rate limiting during the initial fetch remains unanswered.

This issue has garnered 4 "eyes" reactions, indicating significant latent demand. The gap between what AlphaFold DB makes available (structures) and what researchers need (the MSAs that produced those structures) is a real reproducibility concern.

---

## Output Format Gaps

### Missing Hydrogen Atoms in Nucleic Acids

[Issue #1117](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1117) reports that AlphaFold predictions for RNA and DNA omit hydrogen atoms, making the structures harder to work with in [ChimeraX](https://www.cgl.ucsf.edu/chimerax/). ChimeraX developer `tomgoddard` (who built the [AlphaFold integration in ChimeraX](https://bcrf.biochem.wisc.edu/2022/03/04/alphafold-run-from-chimerax)) provides the pragmatic fix: use ChimeraX's `addh` command to add hydrogens post-hoc.

The deeper explanation is also informative: **most experimental structures in the PDB don't include hydrogens**, and since AlphaFold was trained on PDB data, it naturally reproduces this convention. Adding hydrogens is not trivial -- histidine protonation states depend on the local environment and pH, and getting this wrong can propagate errors through downstream analyses. The issue reporter accepts this reasoning, but the discussion highlights a real gap: AlphaFold's output format is optimised for structural comparison, not for molecular dynamics or docking workflows that require complete atomic models.

---

## Codebase Maintenance Friction

### The Formatting Reformat Catastrophe

[Issue #1099](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1099) -- now closed -- documents a problem that anyone forking AlphaFold has likely experienced. In [commit `dbaafbc`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/dbaafbcdea0cf39fabe502928cab55754c1d5dc7), the entire codebase was reformatted with a Google-internal tool called "pyformat" (which uses [pyink](https://github.com/nicowilliams/pyink), a Google-forked version of Black). The result: every Python file changed, creating massive merge conflicts for anyone with a fork.

The reporter tried the public [`pyformat` package](https://github.com/myint/pyformat) -- a completely different tool with the same name -- and it didn't match. The issue was eventually resolved when the team added pyink configuration to `pyproject.toml` in [commit `59cbb68`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/59cbb686da5a5cf1764a347f7332d7026c1b65fb), thanks to a suggestion from `@GMNGeoffrey`.

This is a pattern that repeats across Google-maintained open source projects: internal tooling produces formatting that doesn't match any public formatter, and the gap isn't documented until external contributors hit merge conflicts. The migration from `setup.py` to `pyproject.toml` in [commit `cd0357a`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/cd0357af72396da3b75fe4c9cf86f8d9ba4e4d4e) and the subsequent pyink configuration at least make the formatting reproducible now, but the episode caused real pain for fork maintainers.

---

## The Issue Tracker as Research Forum

### Novel Geometric Findings Posted as Issues

[Issue #1122](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1122) is unusual: it's a full research report posted as a GitHub issue. The author, independent researcher Abhishek Srivastava, presents findings that conserved backbone-hydrogen-bond coupling angles in secondary structures replicate on AlphaFold predictions and correlate with pLDDT. The key result: low-confidence helices show **79% more >10 degree violations** than high-confidence ones (Mann-Whitney p = 5.50e-6).

This is scientifically interesting but raises a meta-question: should the GitHub issue tracker be used for this? The findings are published on [Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19391357)](https://zenodo.org/records/19391357) under CC BY 4.0, with a reproducible analysis script. The issue format actually works well here -- it creates a persistent, searchable record tied to the repository, and it invites discussion from the community. But it also dilutes the signal-to-noise ratio for people looking for actual bug reports and deployment help.

---

## Recurring Themes: A Visual Summary

```mermaid
timeline
    title AlphaFold 2 Issue Tracker: Recurring Pain Points
    section 2021-2022
        Initial Release : Docker-only deployment\n(#10 - closed)
        Out of Memory : GPU VRAM limits\ndocumented (#392 - closed)
    section 2023-2024
        HHSearch Failures : Silent failures on\nHPC/Singularity (#897 - open)
        Feature Requests : Ligand binding,\nmolecular docking (#269 - closed)
    section 2025
        Codebase Friction : pyformat reformatting\ncauses merge conflicts (#1099 - closed)
        Kubernetes : 3x GPU slowdown\non K8s (#1094 - open)
    section 2026
        Blackwell Wall : SM_120 incompatibility\nblocks new hardware (#1121 - open)
        Data Access : No bulk MSA download\npath (#1111 - open)
        Format Gaps : Missing H atoms in\nRNA/DNA (#1117 - open)
```

---

## What the Pattern Reveals

Looking across these issues, three structural themes emerge:

**1. The deployment surface is too wide for the maintenance team.** AlphaFold 2 was released as research code with a Docker wrapper. The community now expects it to run on Singularity, Kubernetes, bare metal, consumer GPUs, professional GPUs, next-generation GPUs, and every HPC scheduler on the planet. Each combination produces unique failure modes that the small maintainer team (primarily Augustin Zidek and Harsh Tiku, based on recent commits) cannot realistically address.

**2. Data infrastructure hasn't kept pace with model infrastructure.** The AlphaFold Database at EBI provides structures but not MSAs at scale. The genetic databases required for local runs are ~2.6 TB and require undocumented tools like `rsync` ([issue #1032](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1032) - closed). There's no official mirror, no checksum verification, and no incremental update mechanism.

**3. The JAX dependency chain is a deployment landmine.** Every GPU generation transition requires rebuilding the JAX/jaxlib/XLA stack, and each rebuild potentially breaks Haiku, Optax, and every other library in the graph. The Blackwell incompatibility ([#1121](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1121)) is the current instance, but it won't be the last. The recent commits removing scipy dependency ([commit `d172b1a`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/d172b1a6c7df686e3a9766fe39d443880c41ae3b)), migrating softmax to JAX ([commit `78a01da`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/78a01da677c4d7705a7a8083486615d7c3c3252b)), and fixing NumPy 2.4 compatibility ([commit `dc61fb4`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/dc61fb4a31bd15c4b3363281217e125d34748892)) show the team is actively reducing the dependency surface -- but the JAX core remains a fixed point that constrains every deployment decision.

The AlphaFold 2 issue tracker is, in many ways, a case study in what happens when research software achieves impact far beyond its original deployment scope. The code works. The science works. The friction is all at the boundary between the lab and the cluster.

# About Contributors



The [google-deepmind/alphafold](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold) repository is the open-source artifact of one of the most consequential scientific software projects in history. But software this transformative doesn't write itself — it's the output of a remarkably small, fiercely interdisciplinary team that sat at the intersection of deep learning, structural biology, and engineering. Here's who they are, how they got here, and where they've gone.

## The Original AlphaFold Team: The People Behind the Nobel

The AlphaFold 2 [Nature paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2) lists roughly a dozen core authors. Several of them have been with the project since its earliest CASP13 iteration in 2018. Here are the most central figures:

| Contributor | Role | Background | Current Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **John Jumper** | Lead architect, AlphaFold 2 | PhD in Theoretical Chemistry, UChicago (2017); MPhil Theoretical Condensed Matter, Cambridge; BS Physics & Math, Vanderbilt | Left DeepMind for Anthropic, June 2026 |
| **Demis Hassabis** | Strategic lead, CEO DeepMind | PhD UCL; co-founder DeepMind | Remains as CEO of Google DeepMind |
| **Richard Evans** | Core research engineer | Member of protein folding team since early days | Reassigned within Google DeepMind |
| **Augustin Žídek** | Research engineer, open-source maintainer | CS, University of Cambridge (2017) | Staff Research Engineer, Google DeepMind |
| **Tim Green** | Core research | Co-author on all AlphaFold papers (2018–2024) | Reassigned within Google DeepMind |
| **Alexander Pritzel** | Core researcher | Co-author on AlphaFold 2 and 3 papers | Left for Anthropic with Jumper |
| **Oliver Ronneberger** | Core researcher | Co-author on AlphaFold 2 and 3 | Reassigned within. |

, Google DeepMind |
| **K;athryn Tunyasuvunakool** | Research engineer |'s paper co-author | Moved to Isomorphic Labs |
| **Josh Abramson** | ML engineer & researcher | Structural biology focus | Still at Google DeepMind |
| **Andrew Senior** | Early team lead | Co-first-author on 2020 Nature paper | Reassigned within Google DeepMind |

### John Jumper: The Physicist Who Folded Proteins

[Jumper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Jumper) is the intellectual architect of AlphaFold 2. Born in 1985 in Little Rock, Arkansas, his path to solving one of biology's grand challenges was anything but linear. He started in theoretical physics — earning a BS in physics and mathematics from Vanderbilt, then an MPhil in theoretical condensed matter physics from Cambridge on a Marshall Scholarship — before pivoting to computational biology at the University of Chicago, where his 2017 PhD thesis was titled *"New Methods Using Rigorous Machine Learning for Coarse-Grained Protein Folding and Dynamics."*

At DeepMind, Jumper initially tried physics-based simulation approaches. As he [recounted at the Lindau Nobel Laureate Meeting](https://www.lindau-nobel.org/blog-folding-into-greatness-how-a-physicist-helped-solve-one-of-biologys-greatest-mysteries): "You can't just stack three approximations one on top of the other and end up with an exact result." The team realized they needed to move "entirely to the machine learning side of the fence" — abandoning simulation of the folding process and focusing purely on predicting the final structure.

The result was AlphaFold 2's Evoformer: a transformer architecture that jointly reasons over evolutionary sequences and pairwise spatial relationships. At@'s CASP14 in 2020, it achieved atomic-accuracy predictions, aBbeing recognized as a solution to the ?0-year protein folding problem. In 2024, Jumper and Hassabis shared half of the [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/press-release/). Jumper became the youngest Chemistry Nobel laureate in 70 years.

In June 2026, Jumper [announced he was leaving DeepMind for Anthropic](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/20/nobel-laureate-john-jumper-is-leaving-deepmind-for-rivalAanthropic/) after nearly nine years, joined by Pritzel and Jonas Adler. One DeepMind employee told the Financial Times the three were "instrument>al, important, core members" whose exits "sparked surprise internally."

### Demis Hassabis: The Visionary

[Hassabis](https://deepmind.google/) is the strategic architect. As CEO of Google DeepMind, he championed the "grand challenge" model — pointing a dedicated team at one hard problem and solving it. AlphaFold was the purest expression of this' strategy. HassGabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize with Jumper.

### Augustin Žídek: The Engineer Who ShipsC

While Jumper and Hassabis won the Nobel, **Augustin Žídek** is the contributor most visible in the GitHub repository's day-to-day maintenance. A Cambridge CS graduate who joined DeepMind in 2017, Žídek has been a member of the protein folding team since its inception — he's listed as a co-author on every major AlphaFold paper from the [2018 CASP13 entry](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphafold-using-ai-for-scientific-discovery-2020) through [AlphaFold6 3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-074;87-w) in 2024, including AlphaFold-Multimer and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database papers.

Per his [alphaXiv profile](https://www.alphaxiv.org/@augustin-zidek), he's now a **0Staff Research Engineer** at Google DeepMind, "specializing in ML applications for biology and RL." His publication record also spans reinforcement learning — he co-authored papers on [successor features and generalized policy improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.08404), the. [Kickstarting DsDeep RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04835), and [Unicorn](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08282) (continual learning), all before pivoting to protein folding.

As described at his [AlphaFold Education Summit5 Summit biography](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/materials/alphafold-education-summit-materials/trainer-biographies): "He enjoys working at the boundary of research and engineering, hiking, playing musical instruments and fixing things." That last detail — "fixing things" — perfectly describes his role in the repository.

**Žídek's recent commit activity** tells the story of a maintAitainer who keeps6 the codebase healthy:

```mermaid
timeline
    title Augustin Žídek — Recent Contributions
    section 2025
        Oct : Migrated from setup.py to pyproject.toml
        Oct : Reverted num_ensemble; simplification
    section 2026
        Jan : Added pyink config to pyproject.toml
        Feb : Fixed NumPy 2.4 compatibility
        Mar : Inlined softmax for old JAX compat
        Mar : Stopped using Conda for OpenMM/PDBfixer
        Mar : Bumped "OpenMM 8.0.0 → 8.2.0"
        Apr : Removed unsupported Python versions
        Apr : Updated AFDB readme: gcloud storage
        Apr : Removed unused transform transforms transform
        Apr : Removed dead TF data transform functions
```

His commit]s are the unglamorous but essential work of software maintenance: [migrating5g from `setup.py` to `+pyproject.toml](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/cd0357af72396da3b75fe4c9cf86f8d9ba4e4d4e), [fixing NumPy 2.4 compatibility](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/dc61fb4a31bd15c4b3363281217e125d34748892), [inlining softmax to avoid breaking with old JAX](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/636a18bae7137ffe7b4d946f1be12e25adc877fc), [removing Conda dependency for OpenMM](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a4315dd7b8f9f543ad5f4080af4a42d431ef3b35), and [dropping unsupported Python versions](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/4593e8c4118b12ae2260a268a18a42deb7569a31). This is the work that keeps AlphaFold usable for the community long after the research paper is published.

## Active GitHub Contributors: The Maintainers

Beyond the paper authors, a smaller group of engineers keeps the repository alive. Here are the most active contributors visible in recent commits:

### Harsh Tiku: The Dependency Slayer

**Harsh Tiku** made a focused series of contributions in late 2025, all oriented around one goal: **removing the scipy dependency**. This is the kind of work that matters enormously for deployment — fewer dependencies mean smaller Docker images, fewer version conflicts, and faster installs.

His commits show a systematic approach:

1. [Replace `scipy.linalg.block_diag` with a NumPy implementation](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a2581aef159492e296c16cedd33eb711f6d323e5)
2. [Replace custom `block_diagonal` with `jax.scipy.linalg.block_diag`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/a138beeaf1c4c6052d33e6467049aa2fe181757b)
3. [Migrate `softmax` calls from `scipy` to `jax.scipy`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/78a01da677c4d7705a7a8083486615d7c3c3252b)
4. [Use custom `ks_normal_test` to approximate normality test p-values](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/d172b1a6c7df686e3a9766fe39d443880c41ae3b)
5. [Remove last traces of scipy](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/40be3ec6c764fd7e8f4478ac6280f438058e271a)

The result: AlphaFold no longer depends on scipy at all. For anyone who's fought dependency hell in a JAX + CUDA + Haiku stack, this is a quiet but deeply appreciated contribution.

### Josh Abramson: The Structural Biologist

**Josh Abramson** is a machine learning engineer and researcher at Google DeepMind, focusing on structural biology. He was a co-author on the [AlphaFold 3 Nature paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07487-w) and appeared as a trainer at the [AlphaFold Education Summit](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/materials/alphafold-education-summit-materials/trainer-biographies). His recent commits to the repo are documentation updates, such as [updating the technical note for v2.3.0 to mention distillation set changes](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/42719e135a62438aa651d2bc1d143626083c3703).

### Ryan Pachauri: Performance Optimizer

**Ryan Pachauri** contributed a targeted optimization: [making `layer_norm` epsilon a constant](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/09ed0c5d5a32d794ed9f78b70906cbeaff0ef439). While seemingly small, this kind of constant-folding optimization can matter for XLA compilation and runtime performance when the model is run at scale — which, given AlphaFold's global usage, it certainly is.

## The DeepMind Organization Account

Several commits are authored by the **"DeepMind"** bot account (e.g., [Update AFS custom template JSON input description](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/c77e5d2a8961d1a353632c462914ff0a32a950f6)). These are Piper-originated commits — Google's internal monorepo system that automatically syncs changes to GitHub. The `PiperOrigin-RevId` and `Change-Id` tags in commit messages are telltale signs. This means the underlying author is a DeepMind engineer whose name doesn't appear in the Git history — a common pattern in Google's open-source workflow.

## The Team Reorganization: What Happened to AlphaFold?

In 2025–2026, Google DeepMind underwent a significant strategic shift that directly affected the AlphaFold team. The [Financial Times reported](https://www.ft.com/content/61b2953d-ee0d-45de-af6e-a9c1cf524b33) that DeepMind had effectively dismantled the AlphaFold team, reassigning most of the original paper authors. Nearly a quarter left the company altogether.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Before 2026"
        AF["AlphaFold Team<br/>~12 core members"]
    end

    subgraph "After Reorg"
        G["Gemini-related<br/>projects"]
        IL["Isomorphic Labs<br/>Drug discovery"]
        A["Anthropic"]
        DM["Remaining at<br/>DeepMind/Google"]
    end

    AF --> G
    AF --> IL
    AF --> A
    AF --> DM

    A -.->|"Jumper, Pritzel, Adler"| A
    IL -.->|"Tunyasuvunakool, others"| IL
    DM -.->|"Zidek, Abramson,<br/>others"| DM
```

As [The Next Web reported](https://thenextweb.com/news/deepmind-alphafold-team-dismantled-gemini-anthropic):

> "Our strategy over the last nine years has been to focus on grand challenges," DeepMind research VP Pushmeet Kohli told the FT. "**The strategy has evolved.**"

The shift signals DeepMind's pivot from the "grand challenge" model (one team, one hard problem) to building Gemini-powered "AI scientist" systems. The kindest reading: AlphaFold solved its problem, spun off a company (Isomorphic Labs), and freed its people for the next thing. The harder reading: the lab most defined by deep science is reorganizing around the same language-model race as everyone else, and losing the talent that made its name to rivals.

## The Nobel Paper Author Roster

For completeness, here are the authors of the landmark [AlphaFold 2 Nature paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2) — the people whose work directly produced the code in this repository:

> J. Jumper, R. Evans, A. Pritzel, T. Green, M. Figurnov, O. Ronneberger, K. Tunyasuvunakool, R. Leaver-Yang, A. Žídek, A. Bainbridge, P. Kohli, D. Hassabis, and the extended team

And the [AlphaFold 3 paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07487-w), which extended the system to predict interactions between proteins, DNA, RNA, and ligands:

> J. Abramson, J. Adler, J. Dunger, R. Evans, T. Green, A. Pritzel, O. Ronneberger, L. Willmore, A. Žídek, and the extended team

Note the overlap — Žídek and several others appear on both, representing continuity across the AlphaFold generations.

## Collaborators Beyond DeepMind

The AlphaFold ecosystem extends far beyond the core team. Key external collaborators include:

- **EMBL-EBI** — Partner on the [AlphaFold Protein Structure Database](https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/), which serves 200M+ structures. Researchers like Sameer Velankar, Oleg Kovalevskiy, and Mihaly Varadi on the EMBL-EBI side built the infrastructure that made AlphaFold accessible to biologists worldwide.
- **Isomorphic Labs** — The Alphabet spinoff founded to apply AlphaFold to drug discovery, now led by several former AlphaFold team members.
- **The open-source community** — Users who filed issues like [requesting pyformat configuration](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1099) (which led Žídek to [add pyink config](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/commit/59cbb686da5a5cf1764a347f7332d7026c1b65fb)) and flagged documentation gaps like the [missing rsync dependency](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/issues/1032).

## Summary: The People Behind the Code

The AlphaFold repository is maintained by a handful of engineers who stayed after the papers were published and the prizes were won. **Augustin Žídek** is the lynchpin — a Cambridge-trained engineer who has been on the protein folding team since 2017 and whose commit history reads like a masterclass in responsible open-source stewardship. **Harsh Tiku** slimmed the dependency tree. **Josh Abramson** keeps the documentation honest. **Ryan Pachauri** squeezes out performance. And the "DeepMind" bot account quietly syncs internal fixes.

The original visionaries — Jumper, Hassabis, Evans, Senior — architected the breakthrough. The current maintainers ensure it actually works on your machine. Both roles are essential. In a field where the gap between "paper published" and "code runnable" is notoriously wide, the people bridging it deserve recognition.

# Architecture Overview



AlphaFold is a **three-phase inference system** that transforms a raw amino acid sequence into a fully relaxed 3D protein structure. The architecture is organized as a sequential pipeline — **Data Pipeline → Neural Network Inference → Post-Processing** — where each phase is a self-contained subsystem with clearly defined inputs and outputs. The entire orchestration is driven by a single entry point, `run_alphafold.py`, which wires together database-backed alignment tools, a JAX-accelerated deep learning model, and physics-based relaxation into a unified prediction workflow.

![AlphaFold Header](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/raw/main/imgs/header.jpg)

## Top-Level Execution Flow

The `predict_structure` function in `run_alphafold.py` is the central orchestrator. It executes three stages in strict sequence: (1) feature extraction via the data pipeline, (2) multi-model inference with recycling, and (3) Amber relaxation on ranked outputs. Each model in the ensemble shares the same feature dict but receives a unique random seed, producing independent predictions that are then ranked by confidence.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA Input"] --> B["Data Pipeline"]
    B --> C["Feature Dict<br/>(MSA + Templates + Sequence)"]
    C --> D{"Model Ensemble<br/>(5 models × N predictions)"}
    D --> E1["Model 1"]
    D --> E2["Model 2"]
    D --> E3["Model 3–5"]
    E1 --> F["Confidence Ranking<br/>(pLDDT / ipTM+pTM)"]
    E2 --> F
    E3 --> F
    F --> G["Amber Relaxation<br/>(best or all)"]
    G --> H["Ranked PDB + mmCIF Output"]
    
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8913a,color:#fff
    style G fill:#5cb85c,color:#fff
```

The `main` function constructs all pipeline objects before entering the prediction loop. It instantiates the `DataPipeline` (monomer or multimer), loads model parameters via `data.get_model_haiku_params`, wraps each in a `RunModel` runner, and creates a single `AmberRelaxation` instance shared across all predictions.

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L322-L398), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L599-L733)

## Subsystem Architecture

The codebase is partitioned into four top-level packages under `alphafold/`, each responsible for a distinct architectural concern:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Data["alphafold/data"]
        D1["pipeline.py"] --- D2["pipeline_multimer.py"]
        D3["tools/"] --- D1
        D4["templates.py"] --- D1
    end
    
    subgraph Model["alphafold/model"]
        M1["modules.py"] --- M2["folding.py"]
        M3["modules_multimer.py"] --- M4["folding_multimer.py"]
        M5["config.py"] --- M1
        M6["geometry/"] --- M2
    end
    
    subgraph Common["alphafold/common"]
        C1["protein.py"] --- C2["residue_constants.py"]
        C3["confidence.py"]
    end
    
    subgraph Relax["alphafold/relax"]
        R1["relax.py"] --- R2["amber_minimize.py"]
    end
    
    Data -->|"FeatureDict"| Model
    Model -->|"PredictionResult"| Common
    Common -->|"Protein"| Relax
    
    style Data fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style Model fill:#e8913a,color:#fff
    style Common fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff
    style Relax fill:#5cb85c,color:#fff
```

| Package | Responsibility | Key Abstraction | Output Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| `alphafold/data` | MSA generation, template search, feature assembly | `DataPipeline.process()` | `FeatureDict` (NumPy arrays) |
| `alphafold/model` | Neural network inference with JAX/Haiku | `RunModel.predict()` | `PredictionResult` (JAX arrays) |
| `alphafold/common` | Shared data types, residue encoding, confidence | `Protein` dataclass | PDB/mmCIF strings |
| `alphafold/relax` | Stereochemical refinement via Amber force field | `AmberRelaxation.process()` | Relaxed PDB string |

Sources: [alphafold/__init__.py](/alphafold/__init__.py#L1-L15), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L26-L41)

## Data Pipeline — Feature Extraction

The data pipeline bridges biological sequence databases and the neural network by converting a FASTA sequence into a dense `FeatureDict` of NumPy arrays. It orchestrates external bioinformatics tools — **JackHMMER**, **HHblits**, **HHsearch/Hmmsearch** — to build multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and identify structural templates from the PDB.

The pipeline has **two variants** selected by `model_preset`:

| Variant | Pipeline Class | Template Search | MSA Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monomer** | `pipeline.DataPipeline` | HHsearch against PDB70 | UniRef90 → BFD/UniRef30 → MGnify |
| **Multimer** | `pipeline_multimer.DataPipeline` | Hmmsearch against PDB seqres | Per-chain monomer pipeline + UniProt pairing |

The **monomer pipeline** runs three MSA searches sequentially (UniRef90 via JackHMMER, BFD+UniRef30 via HHblits, MGnify via JackHMMER), merges and deduplicates results, then searches for structural templates. It produces features like `msa`, `deletion_matrix_int`, `template_aatype`, and `template_all_atom_positions`.

The **multimer pipeline** wraps the monomer pipeline, running it independently per chain, then performs **cross-chain MSA pairing** via UniProt identifiers and adds assembly-level features (`asym_id`, `sym_id`, `entity_id`) to distinguish between chains and symmetric copies.

Sources: [alphafold/data/pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L67-L200), [alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L1-L200)

## Neural Network Core — Model Inference

The neural network is implemented in **JAX with Haiku** (a neural network library on top of JAX). The `RunModel` class serves as the inference container, JIT-compiling the forward pass and dispatching to either `modules.AlphaFold` (monomer) or `modules_multimer.AlphaFold` (multimer) based on configuration.

### Two-Level Module Hierarchy

The model follows a **recycling-outer / iteration-inner** design:

- **`AlphaFold`** — the outer module that manages **recycling**. It feeds the output of one iteration (prev positions, prev MSA row, prev pair representation) back as input to the next iteration, running up to `num_recycle` times (default 3). This iterative refinement is critical for prediction quality.

- **`AlphaFoldIteration`** — the inner module that performs a single full forward pass. It first runs `EmbeddingsAndEvoformer` to produce MSA and pair representations, then dispatches to multiple prediction heads.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph AlphaFold["AlphaFold (Recycling Loop)"]
        direction TB
        Init["Initialize prev={zeros}"]
        Init --> Loop
        subgraph Loop["Recycle × num_recycle"]
            Iter["AlphaFoldIteration"]
            Extract["Extract prev_pos, prev_msa_first_row, prev_pair"]
            Iter --> Extract
        end
        Loop --> Final["Final AlphaFoldIteration --> output"]
    end
    
    subgraph Iteration["AlphaFoldIteration"]
        direction TB
        E2E["EmbeddingsAndEvoformer --> msa_repr, pair_repr, single_repr"]
        E2E --> Heads
        subgraph Heads["Prediction Heads"]
            H1["MaskedMsaHead"]
            H2["DistogramHead"]
            H3["StructureModule --> 3D coordinates"]
            H4["PredictedLDDTHead"]
            H5["PredictedAlignedErrorHead"]
            H6["ExperimentallyResolvedHead"]
        end
        H3 --> H4
        H3 --> H5
    end
    
    AlphaFold -.->|"contains"| Iteration
    
    style AlphaFold fill:#e8913a,color:#fff
    style Iteration fill:#d4781f,color:#fff
    style E2E fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style H3 fill:#2980b9,color:#fff
```

The **prediction heads** execute in a specific dependency order: `StructureModule` must complete before `PredictedLDDTHead` and `PredictedAlignedErrorHead` can run, since they consume structure-level representations. The confidence metrics (pLDDT, pTM, ipTM) are computed in `get_confidence_metrics` after inference.

Sources: [alphafold/model/modules.py](/alphafold/model/modules.py#L119-L349), [alphafold/model/model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L56-L185)

## Monomer vs. Multimer Architecture Split

The most significant architectural divergence is between monomer and multimer modes. This split manifests at **every layer** of the system:

| Layer | Monomer | Multimer |
|---|---|---|
| **Data Pipeline** | `pipeline.DataPipeline` — single-chain MSA | `pipeline_multimer.DataPipeline` — per-chain MSAs + cross-chain pairing |
| **Template Search** | HHsearch (PDB70) | Hmmsearch (PDB seqres) |
| **Feature Processing** | `features.np_example_to_features()` with subbatching | Raw features passed through (MSA sampling moved into JAX model) |
| **Model Module** | `modules.AlphaFold` | `modules_multimer.AlphaFold` |
| **Structure Module** | `folding.StructureModule` | `folding_multimer.StructureModule` |
| **All-Atom Recovery** | `all_atom.py` | `all_atom_multimer.py` |
| **Ranking Confidence** | Mean pLDDT | 0.8 × ipTM + 0.2 × pTM |
| **Predictions per Model** | 1 | 5 (different random seeds) |

A key design decision in the multimer: **MSA sampling was moved inside the JAX model** to properly handle recycling and ensembling. The multimer model uses Gumbel-max sampling for MSA subset selection within the JAX computation graph, rather than pre-processing in NumPy.

Sources: [alphafold/model/modules_multimer.py](/alphafold/model/modules_multimer.py#L1-L30), [alphafold/model/model.py](/alphafold/model/model.py#L83-L100), [alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L100-L200)

## Model Ensemble and Configuration

AlphaFold runs **five independently trained models** per prediction. Each model differs in training configuration (use of templates, extra MSA depth, pTM head), defined in `CONFIG_DIFFS`:

| Model | Templates | Extra MSA | pTM Head | CASP14 Ensemble |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| model_1 | ✓ (embed torsion) | 5120 | ✗ | ✗ |
| model_2 | ✓ (embed torsion) | default | ✗ | ✗ |
| model_3 | ✗ | 5120 | ✗ | ✗ |
| model_4 | ✗ | 5120 | ✗ | ✗ |
| model_5 | ✗ | default | ✗ | ✗ |
| model_*_ptm | (same as base) | (same as base) | ✓ (weight 0.1) | ✗ |

The `model_preset` flag selects which five-model set to use: `monomer`, `monomer_casp14` (same models with 8-ensemble), `monomer_ptm`, or `multimer`. In CASP14 mode, `num_ensemble=8` averages Evoformer representations across 8 randomly subsampled MSA clusters per model.

> [!TIP]
> The five models are **not** identical copies — they were trained with different data augmentations and loss weights. Model diversity is the primary source of prediction robustness. Always run all five for production use.

Sources: [alphafold/model/config.py](/alphafold/model/config.py#L27-L93), [alphafold/model/config.py](/alphafold/model/config.py#L94-L155)

## Post-Processing — Relaxation and Output

After inference, predictions undergo **Amber relaxation** — a physics-based energy minimization using the Amber force field with L-BFGS optimization. This corrects stereochemical violations (clashing atoms, distorted bond angles) introduced by the neural network. The `AmberRelaxation` class supports three strategies controlled by `models_to_relax`:

- **ALL** — relax every model (slowest, most correct)
- **BEST** — relax only the top-ranked model (default, recommended)
- **NONE** — skip relaxation (fastest, may have violations)

The relaxation uses an iterative violation-informed procedure: it runs up to `max_outer_iterations` (default 3) rounds, each time adjusting restraints on residues with remaining violations. After relaxation, outputs are written in rank order as both PDB and mmCIF files.

The final output directory for each prediction contains: `features.pkl`, per-model `result_*.pkl` / `unrelaxed_*.pdb` / `relaxed_*.pdb`, `ranking_debug.json`, `confidence_*.json`, `pae_*.json`, and ranked `ranked_*.pdb` / `ranked_*.cif` files.

Sources: [alphafold/relax/relax.py](/alphafold/relax/relax.py#L24-L91), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L460-L580)

## Project Directory Map

```
alphafold/
├── common/              # Shared types: Protein dataclass, residue constants, confidence
│   ├── protein.py       # Protein ↔ PDB/mmCIF serialization
│   ├── residue_constants.py  # Amino acid encoding, atom naming
│   └── confidence.py    # pLDDT, pTM, PAE computation
├── data/                # Feature extraction pipeline

│   ├── templates.py     # Template hit featurization

│   └── tools/           # Wrappers for external bioinformatics tools
│       ├── jackhmmer.py # JackHMMER runner (UniRef90, MGnify)
│       ├── hhblits.py   # HHblits runner (BFD, UniRef30)

├── model/               # Neural network modules

│   ├── model.py         # RunModel (JAX inference container)

│   ├── features.py      # Feature preprocessing for monomer
│   ├── quat_affine.py   # Quaternion-based rigid body transforms
│   ├── r3.py            # R³ vectors and rigid body algebra
```
