# MSA Generation Workflow



The Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) generation workflow is AlphaFold's most computationally expensive and architecturally critical preprocessing stage. It transforms a raw amino acid sequence into the evolutionary signal that powers the Evoformer — without a deep, diverse MSA, even the most sophisticated neural architecture cannot recover a protein's 3D structure. This page dissects the complete MSA pipeline: from the external bioinformatics tools that search genetic databases, through the parsers that normalize alignment formats, to the feature assembly logic that deduplicates and merges everything into the NumPy arrays consumed by the model.

## The Central Role of MSA in AlphaFold

AlphaFold's insight is that the co-evolutionary information encoded in an MSA — which positions mutate in concert across evolutionary time — is the strongest signal for inter-residue contacts. The MSA is not merely "homology information"; it is the **primary input representation** for the Evoformer stack, which iteratively refines MSA and pair representations. A shallow MSA (few diverse sequences) yields low-confidence predictions; a deep MSA with broad taxonomic coverage is the difference between a pLDDT of 50 and 95.

The MSA generation workflow is orchestrated by two pipeline classes depending on the prediction mode. The monomer pipeline performs three sequential database searches. The multimer pipeline extends this with per-chain searches and a cross-chain pairing step that stitches together evolutionary information from complex subunits.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L123-L173), [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L184-L216)

## Monomer MSA Pipeline Architecture

The `DataPipeline` class in `pipeline.py` is the monomer's central orchestrator. It constructs three MSA runner instances at initialization and executes them in a fixed order during `process()`. The following diagram shows the complete flow from FASTA input to the merged feature dictionary:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA Input<br/>(single sequence)"] --> B["Jackhmmer<br/>+ UniRef90"]
    A --> C["Jackhmmer<br/>+ MGnify"]
    A --> D{"use_small_bfd?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["Jackhmmer<br/>+ small_BFD<br/>(.sto output)"]
    D -- No --> F["HHblits<br/>+ BFD + UniRef30<br/>(.a3m output)"]
    
    B --> G["parse_stockholm()"]
    C --> G
    E --> G
    F --> H["parse_a3m()"]
    
    G --> I["make_msa_features()<br/>Deduplicate + Merge"]
    H --> I
    
    B --> J["Deduplicate +<br/>Remove Empty Cols"]
    J --> K["Template Search<br/>(HHsearch / Hmmsearch)"]
    
    I --> L["FeatureDict<br/>{msa, deletion_matrix_int,<br/>num_alignments, msa_species_identifiers}"]
    K --> M["Template Features"]
    
    L --> N["Final FeatureDict"]
    M --> N
    
    style A fill:#4a9eff,color:#fff
    style N fill:#2ecc71,color:#fff
    style I fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
```

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L174-L280)

### The Three Database Searches

Each database search targets a different level of the evolutionary tree, and together they provide broad coverage:

| Search Step | Tool | Database | Output Format | Default Max Hits | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jackhmmer | UniRef90 | Stockholm (.sto) | 10,000 | Clustered UniProt reference — broad evolutionary coverage |
| 2 | Jackhmmer | MGnify | Stockholm (.sto) | 501 | Metagenomic sequences — environmental/uncultured organisms |
| 3a | HHblits | BFD + UniRef30 | A3M (.a3m) | unlimited | Deep diversity from big fragmented database (full_dbs preset) |
| 3b | Jackhmmer | small_bfd | Stockholm (.sto) | unlimited | Reduced database for faster execution (reduced_dbs preset) |

The `use_small_bfd` flag (set by `--db_preset=reduced_dbs`) switches between HHblits with the full BFD+UniRef30 databases and Jackhmmer with the smaller clustered BFD. The full configuration is dramatically slower but yields richer MSAs.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L146-L167), [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L236-L255)

## The `run_msa_tool` Abstraction

Both Jackhmmer and HHblits are invoked through the shared `run_msa_tool()` function, which adds a critical caching layer. When `use_precomputed_msas=True`,D` and the output file already exists on disk, the tool execution is skipped entirely and the cached result is read instead4 directly. This makes iterative development and re-runs feasible without re-executing the expensive bioinformatics searches:

```python
def run_msa_tool(
    msa_runner,
    input_fasta_path: str,
    msa_out_path: str,
    msa_format: str,
    use_precomputed_msas: bool,
    max_sto_sequences: Optional[int] = None,
) -> Mapping[str, Any]:
```

The function also handles truncation of Stockholm-format MSAs to `max_sto_sequences` — this limits the UniRef90 search to 10,000 sequences and MGnify to 501 sequences. A3M-format results from HHblits are not truncated at this stage.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L94-L120)

## Jackhmmer: Iterative HMM Search

Jackhmmer (from HMMER3) performs **iterative profile HMM searches** — each iteration builds a profile from the current hits and searches again, discovering increasingly remote homologs. AlphaFix configures it with a single iteration (`n_iter=1`) by default, relying on the database clustering to handle diversity. Key configuration parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `n_cpu` | 8 | Parallel threads (diminishing returns above 8) |
| `n_iter` | 1 | Number of iterative search rounds |
| `e_value` | 0.0001 | Inclusion threshold — sequences with E-value > this are excluded |
| `filter_f1` | 0.0005 | MSV/biased composition pre-filter proportion |
| `filter_f2` | 0.00005 | Viterbi pre-filter proportion |
| `filter_f3` | 0.0000005 | Forward pre-filter proportion |

The aggressively low filter values (`F1/F2/F3`) are intentional — they trade sensitivity for speed, which is critical for the massive MGnify database. The `_query_chunk()` method constructs the command-line invocation, executes it as a subprocess, and reads the Stockholm output. For chunked streaming (used with very large databases), it supports `num_streamed_chunks` to process the database in segments.

Sources: [jackhmmer.py](/alphafold/data/tools/jackhmmer.py#L31-L169)

## HHblits: HMM-HMM Alignment

HHblits (from HH-suite) performs **HMM-HMM comparison**, which is more sensitive than HMM-sequence comparison because it compares entire profile distributions rather than single sequences. This makes it the preferred tool for the deep BFD database. Key distinctions from Jackhmmer:

- **Output format**: A3M (not Stockholm) — lower-case letters encode insertions relative to the query
- **Multiple databases**: Searches BFD and UniRef30 simultaneously via `-d` flags
- **Default iterations**: 3 (vs. Jackhmmer's 1) — the more sensitive algorithm benefits from iteration
- **No max_sequences truncation**: Returns all hits passing the E-value threshold

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `n_cpu` | 4 | Parallel threads |
| `n_iter` | 3 | Iterative search rounds |
| `e_value` | 0.001 | E-value inclusion threshold |
| `maxseq` | 1,000,000 | Max rows in input alignment |
| `realign_max` | 100,000 | Max HMM-HMM hits to realign |
| `p` | 20 | Minimum probability for inclusion in output |

Sources: [hhblits.py](/alphafold/data/tools/hhblits.py#L32-L163)

## MSA Parsing and Format Conversion

The `parsers.py` module defines the `Msa` dataclass — the canonical in-memory representation used throughout the pipeline:

```python
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class Msa:
    sequences: Sequence[str]
    deletion_matrix: DeletionMatrix
    descriptions: Sequence[str]
```

Each field must have identical length (validated in `__post_init__`). The **deletion matrix** is particularly important: `deletion_matrix[i][j]` counts how many residues were deleted from aligned sequence `i` at position `j` relative to the query. This information is preserved as `deletion_matrix_int` in the final features and used by the Evoformer to weight the importance of each MSA row.

Two format-specific parsers populate this dataclass:

- **`parse_stockholm()`** — Reads Stockholm format (used by Jackhmmer). Strips gap columns from the query sequence, computes deletion vectors by comparing each aligned sequence to the query.
- **`parse_a3m()`** — Reads A3M format (used by HHblits). Lower-case characters represent insertions; the parser counts them into the deletion matrix and strips them to produce the aligned sequence.

Additional utility functions clean and transform MSA data before it reaches the feature assembler:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `deduplicate_stockholm_msa()` | Removes duplicate sequences (ignoring insertions w.r.t. query) — applied to UniRef90 before template search |
| `remove_empty_columns_from_stockholm_msa()` | Strips all-gap columns — applied to UniRef90 before template search |
| `convert_stockholm_to_a3m()` | Converts Stockholm to A3M — used when template searcher requires A3M input |
| `truncate_stockholm_msa()` | Reads only the first N sequences from a Stockholm file to limit memory |

Sources: [parsers.py](/alphafold/data/parsers.py#L29-L58), [parsers.py](/alphafold/data/parsers.py#L104-L202), [parsers.py](/alphafold/data/parsers.py#L317-L389)

## Feature Assembly: `make_msa_features`

After parsing, the three independent MSA objects are merged into a single feature dictionary by `make_msa_features()`. This function performs the critical **cross-MSA deduplication** step — a sequence seen in UniRef90 is not duplicated when it also appears in BFD or MGnify:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["UniRef90 MSA"] --> M["make_msa_features()"]
    B["BFD MSA"] --> M
    G["MGnify MSA"] --> M
    M --> D["Deduplicated<br/>seen_sequences set"]
    D --> F["FeatureDict:<br/>msa, deletion_matrix_int,<br/>num_alignments,<br/>msa_species_identifiers"]
```

The function iterates through each MSA in order (UniRef90 → BFD → MGnify), skipping sequences already in `seen_sequences`. For each unique sequence, it:

1. Converts residues to integer IDs via `HHBLITS_AA_TO_ID` mapping
2. Appends the corresponding deletion matrix row
3. Extracts the **species identifier** from the description line via `msa_identifiers.get_identifiers()`

The resulting features include `msa` (integer-coded alignment matrix), `deletion_matrix_int`, `num_alignments` (total unique sequences), and `msa_species_identifiers` (species codes for each row).

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L570-L91), [msa_identifiers.py](/alphafold/data/msa_identifiers.py#L84-L91)

## Species Identification for MSA Pairing

The `msa_identifiers.py` module extracts taxonomic species codes from MSA description lines. These codes are essential for the multimer pipeline's cross-chain pairing logic. The parser handles UniProtKB format identifiers like `tr|A0A146SKV9|A0A146SKV9_FUNHE`, where `FUNHE` is the 5-character species mnemonic. The regex pattern `_UNIPROT_PATTERN` captures the `SpeciesIdentifier` group, which is stored in the feature dict as bytes for efficient numpy operations.

Sources: [msa_identifiers.py](/alphafold/data/msa_identifiers.py#L25-L72)

## Multimer MSA Pipeline: Per-Chain Search and Cross-Chain Pairing

The multimer pipeline (`pipeline_multimer.DataPipeline`) fundamentally extends the monomer workflow. For a heterodimer with chains A and B, it must answer two questions: (1) what is the evolutionary information for each chain independently? and (2) which sequences across chains come from the **same organism** and therefore represent co-evolved partners?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Multi-FASTA Input<br/>(N chains)"] --> B["Per-chain:<br/>Monomer Pipeline"]
    B --> C["Per-chain:<br/>Jackhmmer + UniProt<br/>(unclustered)"]
    C --> D{"Is homomer/<br/>monomer?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["Block-diagonal<br/>MSA merge"]
    D -- No --> F["MSA Pairing<br/>by species"]
    F --> G["create_paired_features()"]
    G --> H["deduplicate_unpaired_sequences()"]
    H --> I["crop_chains()<br/>(MSA_CROP_SIZE=2048)"]
    E --> I
    I --> J["merge_chain_features()"]
    J --> K["process_final()<br/>Correct restypes, masks"]
    K --> L["pad_msa(min_num_seq=512)"]
    L --> M["Final FeatureDict"]
    
    style A fill:#4a9eff,color:#fff
    style M fill:#2ecc71,color:#fff
    style F fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
```

### Per-Chain Monomer Pipeline

Each chain independently runs the full monomer `DataPipeline.process()`, producing its own UniRef90, BFD, and MGnify MSAs. This ensures deep per-chain evolutionary coverage. For homomers (identical sequences), the pipeline runs only once and deep-copies the features.

### UniProt Search for Pairing

For heteromers, an additional Jackhmmer search against the **unclustered UniProt database** is performed per chain (`_all_seq_msa_features()`). This is distinct from the clustered UniRef90 — the unclustered database preserves individual organism entries needed for species-level pairing. Results are truncated to `max_uniprot_hits=50,000` and stored with the `_all_seq` suffix (e.g., `msa_all_seq`, `deletion_matrix_int_all_seq`).

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L218-L267)

## MSA Pairing: Stitching Cross-Chain Evolutionary Signal

The pairing logic in `msa_pairing.py` is the multimer's most distinctive operation. It identifies sequences from the **same species** across different chains' MSAs and aligns them into paired rows — creating a combined MSA where each row represents a potential real-world complex rather than independent subunit homologs.

### The Pairing Algorithm

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["MSAStatistics for<br/>: each6 each chain = (/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L269-L320)"] --> B["toD: pair_sequences()@1<br/>Build species→MSAStatistics<br/>mapping per chain; Collect/10=0.5"]
```

The `pair_sequences()` function operates in three phases:

1. **Species grouping**: For each chain, `MSAStatistics.from_chain_features()` computes per-row species identifiers, sequence similarity to the target, and gap percentage. The `to_species_dict()` method partitions each chain's MSA rows by species.

2. **Cross-chain matching**: For each species present in **two or more chains**, `_match_rows_by_sequence_similarity()` sorts each chain's rows by similarity to its target sequence and pairs them in order. Species present in only one chain are skipped (no pairing signal). Species with >600 sequences in any chain are also skipped (computational guard).

3. **Priority ordering**: `reorder_paired_rows()` sorts paired rows by the number of chains paired (all-chain pairings first), then by the product of row indices (proxy for E-value ranking). This ensures the most informative pairings occupy the top MSA rows.

### Post-Pairing Processing

After pairing, `create_paired_features()` selects the paired row indices from each chain's `_all_seq` features. Then `deduplicate_unpaired_sequences()` removes any unpaired MSA rows that duplicate a paired row — the paired version is always preferred since it carries cross-chain information. Finally, `_concatenate_paired_and_unpaired_features()` stacks the paired MSA above the block-diagonal unpaired MSA, so the Evoformer sees both signals.

Sources: [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L153-L185), [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L256-L319), [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L546-L567)

## MSA Cropping and Final Processing

The `feature_processing.py` module handles the transition from raw merged features to model-ready arrays. The `pair_and_merge()` function orchestrates:

1. **`process_unmerged_features()`** — Converts deletion matrices to float32, computes `deletion_mean` (average deletions per position), and adds dummy atom positions.

2. **`crop_chains()`** — Limits each chain's MSA to `MSA_CROP_SIZE=2048` rows. For paired MSAs, the crop is split: up to `msa_crop_size // 2` paired rows, with the remainder allocated to unpaired rows minus any non-gapped paired rows already included. Templates are cropped to `MAX_TEMPLATES=4`.

3. **`merge_chain_features()`** — For homomers, merges identical chains by concatenating MSA features along the residue dimension (dense MSA). For heteromers, block-diagonalizes unpaired MSA features and concatenates paired features. Computes `cluster_bias_mask` and `bert_mask`.

4. **`process_final()`** — Corrects MSA residue type ordering via `MAP_HHBLITS_AATYPE_TO_OUR_AATYPE`, generates `seq_mask` and `msa_mask`, and filters to `REQUIRED_FEATURES`.

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L74-L107), [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L142-L195)

## Output Artifacts

The MSA pipeline writes intermediate results to `msa_output_dir` for caching and debugging:

| File | Pipeline | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `uniref90_hits.sto` | Monomer | Stockholm MSA from UniRef90 |
| `mgnify_hits.sto` | Monomer | Stockholm MSA from MGnify |
| `bfd_uniref_hits.a3m` | Monomer (full_dbs) | A3M MSA from HHblits |
| `small_bfd_hits.sto` | Monomer (reduced_dbs) | Stockholm MSA from small BFD |
| `pdb_hits.hhr` | Monomer | Template search results |
| `<chain_id>/uniprot_hits.sto` | Multimer | UniProt MSA for pairing |
| `chain_id_map.json` | Multimer | Chain ID → sequence mapping |

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L187-L255), [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L280-L286)

## Performance Characteristics and Tuning

The MSA generation step dominates end-to-end runtime — typically 10–30 minutes for a 300-residue monomer with full databases. Key performance knobs:

| Lever | Effect | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| `--db_preset=reduced_dbs` | Replaces HHblits+BFD+UniRef30 with Jackhmmer+small_bfd | 3–5× faster, slightly shallower MSA |
| `use_precomputed_msas=True` | Skips all tool execution if output files exist | Zero cost on re-runs; stale data risk |
| `mgnify_max_hits` | Limits MGnify sequences (default 501) | Lower = faster but less metagenomic signal |
| `uniref_max_hits` | Limits UniRef90 sequences (default 10,000) | Lower = faster but less diversity |
| `msa_tools_n_cpu` | CPU threads for Jackhmmer/HHblits | Diminishing returns above 8 |

> [!TIP]
> When debugging MSA quality, check the logged output: `Uniref90 MSA size`, `BFD MSA size`, `MGnify MSA size`, and `Final (deduplicated) MSA size`. A final MSA below ~30 sequences for a typical globular protein signals poor evolutionary coverage and likely low prediction confidence.

> [!TIP]
> In the multimer pipeline, the UniProt search for pairing can be extremely expensive against the full unclustered database. If you only need monomer predictions, use `--model_preset=monomer` to avoid this cost entirely. For multimer, the `max_uniprot_hits=50,000` cap prevents runaway memory usage.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L267-L278), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L160-L167)

## Architectural Summary

The MSA workflow follows a clear **search → parse → merge → pair → crop** pipeline pattern. The monomer path is a three-way fan-out (UniRef90, BFD, MGnify) with a single merge point. The multimer path nests the monomer pipeline per chain, adds a UniProt fan-out for pairing, and introduces a sophisticated species-based pairing algorithm that transforms independent per-chain evolutionary signals into a joint representation capturing inter-chain co-evolution. Both paths converge on the same feature contract — a `FeatureDict` with `msa`, `deletion_matrix_int`, and `num_alignments` arrays — that feeds directly into [Evoformer and Embeddings](11-evoformer-and-embeddings).

The next step in the data pipeline after MSA generation is [Template Search and Featurization](9-template-search-and-featurization), which uses the UniRef90 MSA to find structural homologs in the PDB. For the multimer-specific aspects of feature assembly after MSA pairing, see [Multimer Feature Assembly](10-multimer-feature-assembly).


# Template Search and Featurization



AlphaFold's template pipeline bridges **structural homology search** and **neural network input assembly** — it discovers known PDB structures related to the query sequence and distills their 3D coordinates into fixed-shape NumPy arrays that the Evoformer can consume. The entire flow is orchestrated by `DataPipeline.process()`, which delegates to two collaborating subsystems: a **template searcher** (HHSearch or Hmmsearch) that identifies candidate structures, and a **template featurizer** (`HhsearchHitFeaturizer` or `HmmsearchHitFeaturizer`) that converts raw hits into the six `template_*` feature tensors. Understanding this pipeline is essential for diagnosing why a prediction may lack structural templates or why a specific template was rejected.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L1-L31), [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L1-L34)

## Pipeline Integration: Where Templates Enter the Data Flow

The `DataPipeline` class wires template search into the broader feature assembly. After generating the UniRef90 MSA via Jackhmmer, the pipeline deduplicates and cleans the Stockholm MSA, then feeds it into the template searcher. The searcher returns raw hit strings (`.hhr` or `.dom` format), which are parsed into `TemplateHit` objects and passed to the featurizer. The resulting template features are merged with sequence and MSA features into a single `FeatureDict` returned to the caller.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input FASTA] --> B[Jackhmmer → UniRef90 MSA]
    B --> C[Deduplicate + Remove Empty Columns]
    C --> D{Template Searcher Format?}
    D -->|sto| E[HHSearch.query]
    D -->|a3m| F[Convert Stockholm → A3M<br/>then HHSearch.query]
    E --> G[Raw Hit String]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Parse TemplateHit Objects]
    H --> I[TemplateHitFeaturizer.get_templates]
    I --> J[Template Feature Dict]
    J --> K[Merge with Sequence + MSA Features]
    K --> L[Final FeatureDict to Model]
```

The critical integration code in `DataPipeline.process()` selects the input format, invokes the searcher, parses hits, and calls the featurizer:

```python
# Pipeline feeds UniRef90 MSA to template searcher
if self.template_searcher.input_format == 'sto':
    pdb_templates_result = self.template_searcher.query(msa_for_templates)
elif self.template_searcher.input_format == 'a3m':
    uniref90_msa_as_a3m = parsers.convert_stockholm_to_a3m(msa_for_templates)
    pdb_templates_result = self.template_searcher.query(uniref90_msa_as_a3m)

# Parse raw output into structured TemplateHit objects
pdb_template_hits = self.template_searcher.get_template_hits(
    output_string=pdb_templates_result, input_sequence=input_sequence
)

# Featurize all hits → template feature arrays
templates_result = self.template_featurizer.get_templates(
    query_sequence=input_sequence, hits=pdb_template_hits
)
```

> [!TIP]
> The template searcher operates on the **UniRef90 MSA** (not BFD or MGnify), because HHSearch/Hmmsearch require a profile-style input derived from a diverse but manageable sequence search. Using the deeper BFD MSA would be computationally prohibitive and offers diminishing returns for template identification.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L206-L280), [pipeline.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline.py#L123-L172)

## The Six Template Feature Tensors

The featurizer's output is constrained to exactly six named arrays, defined in the `TEMPLATE_FEATURES` constant. These tensors have a consistent shape aligned to the query sequence length `N_res`, enabling direct consumption by the template embedding stack in the Evoformer.

| Feature Name | Dtype | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `template_aatype` | `float32` | `(T, N_res, 22)` | One-hot amino acid type per residue, mapped via `HHBLITS_AA_TO_ID` (22 classes including gap and X) |
| `template_all_atom_positions` | `float32` | `(T, N_res, 37, 3)` | Cartesian (x,y,z) coordinates for all 37 atom types per residue |
| `template_all_atom_masks` | `float32` | `(T, N_res, 37)` | Binary mask: 1.0 if atom position is experimentally observed, 0.0 if missing |
| `template_domain_names` | `object` | `(T,)` | PDB ID + chain identifier string (e.g. `b"6x2a_A"`) |
| `template_sequence` | `object` | `(T,)` | Aligned template sequence with gaps (`-`) for unaligned query positions |
| `template_sum_probs` | `float32` | `(T,)` | Sum of per-position alignment probabilities from HHSearch, used as a quality/confidence score |

Where `T` is the number of valid templates (up to `max_hits`, typically 4 after downstream filtering). Unaligned query residues receive **zero-filled** atom positions and masks, with `-` in the template sequence — this sparse alignment pattern is exactly what the Evoformer's template attention mechanism learns to exploit.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L88-L95), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L676-L689)

## Hit Prefiltering: Four Gates Before Featurization

Before any mmCIF file is parsed, each `TemplateHit` must pass through `_assess_hhsearch_hit()`, which enforces four sequential prefilter checks. Any failure raises a `PrefilterError` subclass, and the hit is silently skipped (or promoted to a hard error under `strict_error_check`). This prefilter is a **performance optimization** — it avoids expensive mmCIF parsing for obviously invalid hits.

| Check | Exception | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Date cutoff** | `DateError` | `release_date > max_template_date` | Prevents information leakage from structures solved after the query's experimental date |
| **Alignment ratio** | `AlignRatioError` | `aligned_cols / len(query) ≤ 0.1` | Rejects hits covering <10% of the query — too fragmentary to provide useful structural guidance |
| **Duplicate/subsequence** | `DuplicateError` | `template ∈ query ∧ length_ratio > 0.95` | Filters near-identical sequences (e.g., the query itself deposited in PDB) |
| **Minimum length** | `LengthError` | `len(template_sequence) < 10` | Discards trivially short fragments that cannot contribute meaningful 3D constraints |

The **date cutoff** is the most critical gate for CASP-style evaluations — it ensures AlphaFold cannot "cheat" by using structures that were only solved after the prediction deadline. The `max_template_date` is configured at pipeline initialization and enforced both in the prefilter (using a precomputed release dates file) and again after mmCIF parsing (using the actual release date in the mmCIF header).

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L175-L241), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L831-L845)

## Single Hit Processing: The Core Featurization Path

The function `_process_single_hit()` orchestrates the full lifecycle of converting one `TemplateHit` into a feature dictionary. Its logic follows a strict sequence: **identify → prefilter → map → parse → extract → validate**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[TemplateHit] --> B[_get_pdb_id_and_chain]
    B --> C{Obsolete?}
    C -->|Removed from PDB| D[Skip: return None]
    C -->|Replaced| E[Replace PDB code with successor]
    C -->|Valid| F[_assess_hhsearch_hit prefilter]
    E --> F
    F -->|PrefilterError| G[Skip or Error]
    F -->|Pass| H[_build_query_to_hit_index_mapping]
    H --> I[Locate mmCIF file in mmcif_dir]
    I --> J[mmcif_parsing.parse]
    J --> K{Date check from mmCIF header}
    K -->|After cutoff| L[Skip or Error]
    K -->|Valid| M[_extract_template_features]
    M --> N{Sequence found in PDB?}
    N -->|Yes exact| O[Use direct mapping]
    N -->|No| P[_realign_pdb_template_to_query<br/>via Kalign]
    P --> Q{≥90% sequence identity?}
    Q -->|No| R[QueryToTemplateAlignError]
    Q -->|Yes| O
    O --> S[_get_atom_positions]
    S --> T[Map atoms to query indices]
    T --> U[Validate atom mask ≠ all zeros]
    U --> V[Return SingleHitResult with features]
```

### Query-to-Template Index Mapping

The alignment between query and template residues is captured by `_build_query_to_hit_index_mapping()`, which produces a `Mapping[int, int]` — a dictionary from query residue indices to template residue indices. This mapping accounts for the fact that HHSearch reports only the **aligned subsequence** of the query, not the full query. The function computes an offset (`hhsearch_query_offset`) by locating the aligned query fragment within the original query sequence, then pairs each query position with its corresponding template position using the hit's `indices_query` and `indices_hit` arrays.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L763-L904), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L692-L746)

## Template Sequence Matching: Exact → Sequence-Only → Fuzzy

When extracting features from a parsed mmCIF, `_find_template_in_pdb()` attempts three progressively relaxed strategies to locate the template chain within the PDB structure:

1. **Exact match** (chain ID + subsequence): Checks if the template sequence appears as a contiguous substring of the chain with the matching chain ID. This is the fastest and most reliable path.
2. **Sequence-only match**: If the chain ID doesn't match, scans **all chains** in the mmCIF object for a subsequence match. Handles cases where HHSearch reports a different chain ID than what appears in the mmCIF.
3. **Fuzzy match** (wildcard X): Constructs a regex where each template residue matches itself **or** the ambiguity code `X`. This accommodates sequences with unresolved residues that are marked as `X` in the PDB but identified more precisely by HHSearch.

If all three strategies fail, a `SequenceNotInTemplateError` is raised, triggering the **realignment fallback** via `_realign_pdb_template_to_query()`.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L244-L313)

## Realignment: When the mmCIF Sequence Differs from the Hit

A subtle but important edge case arises when PDB70 (the HHsearch database) contains a **different version** of the template sequence than the actual mmCIF file — for example, when the PDB entry was updated or re-refined after PDB70 was built. In this case, `_find_template_in_pdb()` raises `SequenceNotInTemplateError`, and `_extract_template_features()` falls back to realignment:

The realignment procedure uses **Kalign** to align the old template sequence (from the HHSearch hit) against the new template sequence (from the mmCIF file). It then requires **≥90% sequence identity** between the two (measured against the shorter sequence). If this threshold is met, the old query-to-template mapping is composed with the old-to-new mapping to produce a corrected `new_query_to_template_mapping`. If the threshold is not met, a `QueryToTemplateAlignError` is raised — the mmCIF structure has diverged too far from what HHSearch reported, and using it would introduce misleading structural information.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L316-L450), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L600-L628)

## Atom Position Extraction and Validation

The function `_get_atom_positions()` reads all-atom 3D coordinates from the parsed mmCIF structure and produces two arrays:

- **`all_positions`**: Shape `(num_res, 37, 3)` — Cartesian coordinates for each of 37 atom types (N, CA, C, O, CB, ...) per residue.
- **`all_positions_mask`**: Shape `(num_res, 37)` — Binary indicator for whether each atom has experimental coordinates.

Two special atom-handling rules are applied during extraction:

1. **Selenomethionine (MSE)**: The selenium atom (`SE`) coordinates are placed in the **sulphur column** (`SD`), allowing the model to treat MSE like standard methionine without adding a special atom type.
2. **Arginine NH1/NH2 swap**: In some PDB entries, the NH1 and NH2 atom names are incorrectly assigned such that NH2 is closer to CD than NH1. The code detects this geometric inconsistency and swaps the coordinates and masks.

After extraction, `_check_residue_distances()` validates that consecutive **Cα–Cα distances** between unmasked residues do not exceed `max_ca_ca_distance` (set to **150.0 Å** in `_extract_template_features` — effectively infinity, acting as a sanity check for catastrophically malformed structures rather than a strict geometric filter).

> [!TIP]
> The 150.0 Å Cα–Cα distance threshold is intentionally permissive. A normal peptide bond yields ~3.8 Å Cα–Cα spacing. The high threshold avoids rejecting templates with chain breaks or missing residues, which are common in experimental PDB structures. Only genuinely corrupt coordinate data (e.g., serialization errors) would exceed this limit.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L477-L541), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L453-L474), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L630-L639)

## Feature Assembly: Mapping Atoms onto the Query Index Space

The final step in `_extract_template_features()` projects the template's all-atom data onto the **query sequence's index space**. This is where the alignment mapping becomes critical:

```python
# Initialize all positions to zeros (for unaligned residues)
for _ in query_sequence:
    templates_all_atom_positions.append(np.zeros((37, 3)))
    templates_all_atom_masks.append(np.zeros(37))
    output_templates_sequence.append('-')

# Overwrite with template data where alignment exists
for k, v in mapping.items():
    template_index = v + mapping_offset
    templates_all_atom_positions[k] = all_atom_positions[template_index][0]
    templates_all_atom_masks[k] = all_atom_masks[template_index][0]
    output_templates_sequence[k] = template_sequence[v]
```

The key insight: **`k` indexes the query sequence**, while **`v + mapping_offset` indexes the template structure**. Residues in the query that have no corresponding template residue retain their zero-initialized positions and masks — this sparse pattern is how the model learns which structural constraints are available. After assembly, the template sequence is one-hot encoded via `sequence_to_onehot()` using the `HHBLITS_AA_TO_ID` mapping (22 classes), producing the `template_aatype` feature.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L641-L689)

## HhsearchHitFeaturizer vs HmmsearchHitFeaturizer

AlphaFold provides two concrete implementations of the `TemplateHitFeaturizer` abstract class, corresponding to the two supported template search backends:

| Aspect | `HhsearchHitFeaturizer` | `HmmsearchHitFeaturizer` |
|---|---|---|
| **Search backend** | HHSearch (profile HMM vs. profile HMM) | Hmmsearch (profile HMM vs. sequence) |
| **Hit ordering** | Sorted by `sum_probs` descending | Sorted by `sum_probs` descending (if available) |
| **Deduplication** | None (relies on HHSearch to deduplicate) | Tracks `already_seen` set by `template_sequence` key |
| **Empty result handling** | Returns empty array with correct dtype | Returns **default zero-filled template** with shape `(1, N_res, ...)` |
| **Input format** | A3M (via `input_format='a3m'`) | Sto (via `input_format='sto'`) |

The `HmmsearchHitFeaturizer`'s deduplication logic prevents the same template sequence from appearing multiple times under different chain IDs — a common situation in PDB entries with symmetric homomultimers. Its empty-result fallback produces a single dummy template of all zeros rather than an empty array, ensuring downstream tensor shapes remain consistent even when no templates are found.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L914-L983), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L985-L1050), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L1053-L1141)

## Error Handling Philosophy: Warnings vs. Hard Errors

The template pipeline implements a **two-tier error model** controlled by the `strict_error_check` flag:

- **Soft mode** (`strict_error_check=False`, default): Template failures are **warnings** — the hit is silently skipped, and processing continues. This maximizes the number of valid templates returned. Errors like `NoChainsError`, `NoAtomDataInTemplateError`, and `TemplateAtomMaskAllZerosError` are treated as indicators of missing experimental data, not bugs.
- **Strict mode** (`strict_error_check=True`): `DateError` and `DuplicateError` from the prefilter become **hard errors** that propagate to the caller. Feature extraction failures also become errors. This mode is used during validation and testing to ensure template quality.

Both modes collect all errors and warnings into the `TemplateSearchResult` dataclass, preserving a complete audit trail even when processing succeeds.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L788-L904), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L907-L912)

## Obsolete PDB Handling

PDB entries are occasionally deprecated and replaced by newer entries. The `_parse_obsolete()` function reads the PDB's obsolete entries file, which can map an old PDB ID to a replacement ID or to `None` (indicating removal). During hit processing:

1. If the hit's PDB code is obsolete with **no replacement** → skip immediately.
2. If the hit's PDB code is obsolete **with a replacement** → substitute the replacement PDB code before prefiltering and mmCIF lookup.

This ensures the pipeline can still find the correct structural data even when HHSearch returns hits referencing deprecated entries.

Sources: [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L133-L153), [templates.py](/alphafold/data/templates.py#L775-L785)

## From Templates to the Evoformer

The assembled template features flow directly into the Evoformer's **template embedding stack**, where each of the `T` templates is independently embedded and then aggregated via attention. The `template_sum_probs` score weights template influence — higher-probability alignments contribute more strongly to the initial pairwise representation. The sparse `template_all_atom_masks` guide the model to attend only to experimentally observed coordinates, ignoring gaps introduced by alignment.

For the complete picture of how template features interact with the Evoformer's attention mechanisms, see [Evoformer and Embeddings](11-evoformer-and-embeddings). For the multimer-specific template assembly logic, see [Multimer Feature Assembly](10-multimer-feature-assembly).


# Multimer Feature Assembly



AlphaFold's multimer pipeline extends the monomer data pipeline to predict structures of multi-chain protein complexes. The core architectural challenge is **cross-chain MSA pairing** — constructing a joint MSA that captures evolutionary co-variation between interacting chains. This page dissects the three-module assembly system (`pipeline_multimer` → `feature_processing` → `msa_pairing`) that transforms per-chain monomer features into a unified feature dictionary ready for the Evoformer.

## Pipeline Orchestration: From FASTA to Unified Features

The multimer `DataPipeline.process()` method is the top-level entry point. It accepts a multi-sequence FASTA file and produces a single merged `FeatureDict` spanning all chains. The orchestration follows a strict five-phase sequence, where each phase depends on outputs from the prior:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Phase 1: Parse Multi-Chain FASTA<br/>_make_chain_id_map()"] --> B["Phase 2: Per-Chain Monomer Pipeline<br/>_process_single_chain()"]
    B --> C["Phase 3: Feature Conversion<br/>convert_monomer_features()"]
    C --> D["Phase 4: Assembly Annotation<br/>add_assembly_features()"]
    D --> E["Phase 5: Pair & Merge<br/>feature_processing.pair_and_merge()"]
    E --> F["Phase 6: MSA Padding<br/>pad_msa(min_num_seq=512)"]

    B -. "Heteromer only" .-> B2["UniProt jackhmmer search<br/>_all_seq_msa_features()"]
    B2 -. "species identifiers<br/>for pairing" .-> E

    style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#1a73e8
    style E fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
    style F fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#1e8e3e
```

Phase 1 parses the input FASTA and builds a `chain_id_map` — a mapping from PDB-format chain IDs (A, B, C, …) to `_FastaChain` dataclass instances holding each chain's sequence and description. This map is serialized to `chain_id_map.json` for downstream use. The system validates that chain count does not exceed **62** (the PDB format limit, corresponding to `PDB_CHAIN_IDS = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789'`).

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L39-L77), [protein.py](/alphafold/common/protein.py#L34-L35)

## Per-Chain Monomer Processing with UniProt Pairing Features

For each unique sequence in the input, `_process_single_chain()` runs the **standard monomer `pipeline.DataPipeline`** on that chain in isolation — generating uniref90, mgnify, and BFD/UniRef30 MSAs plus template hits via HHsearch/HMMsearch. This reuses the monomer infrastructure unchanged.

Critically, for **heteromers** (where `len(set(input_seqs)) > 1`), an additional UniProt jackhmmer search is performed via `_all_seq_msa_features()`. This unclustered UniProt MSA serves a different purpose than the monomer MSA: it provides **species identifiers** for cross-chain pairing. The method extracts only `msa`, `msa_mask`, `deletion_matrix`, `deletion_matrix_int`, and `msa_species_identifiers` from the UniProt result, suffixing each key with `_all_seq` to distinguish them from the monomer MSA features. Species identifiers are parsed from UniProt description lines using the regex pattern `tr|Accession|EntryName_SpeciesCode` (e.g., `tr|A0A146SKV9|A0A146SKV9_FUNHE` yields species `FUNHE`).

Identical chains (homomeric copies) are handled efficiently: the pipeline checks `sequence_features` cache and deep-copies features for duplicate sequences rather than re-running the expensive monomer pipeline.

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L218-L310), [msa_identifiers.py](/alphafold/data/msa_identifiers.py#L25-L72)

## Monomer-to-Multimer Feature Conversion

`convert_monomer_features()` reshapes per-chain features produced by the monomer pipeline into the format expected by multimer models. The key transformations are:

| Feature | Monomer Format | Multimer Format | Transformation |
|---------|---------------|-----------------|----------------|
| `aatype` | One-hot `(N_res, 21)` | Integer `(N_res,)` | `np.argmax(axis=-1)` |
| `template_aatype` | One-hot `(N_templ, N_res, 21)` | Integer `(N_templ, N_res)` | `argmax` + remap via `MAP_HHBLITS_AATYPE_TO_OUR_AATYPE` |
| `sequence` | Shape `(1,)` object | Scalar object | Squeeze leading dim |
| `domain_name` | Shape `(1,)` object | Scalar object | Squeeze leading dim |
| `num_alignments` | Shape `(N_res,)` | Scalar | Squeeze leading dim |
| `seq_length` | Shape `(N_res,)` | Scalar | Squeeze leading dim |
| `template_all_atom_masks` | Key name with 's' | Renamed to `template_all_atom_mask` | Key rename |

Additionally, `auth_chain_id` is injected as a new feature carrying the PDB chain identifier. The one-hot → integer conversion for `aatype` is significant: the multimer model's embedding layers perform their own one-hot encoding internally, so the pre-encoded representation from the monomer pipeline must be inverted.

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L79-L105)

## Assembly Feature Annotation: Entity, Symmetry, and Asymmetry IDs

`add_assembly_features()` annotates each residue with three integer ID arrays that encode the **structural topology** of the complex:

- **`entity_id`**: Groups chains by identical sequence. Two chains with the same amino acid sequence share an `entity_id`. This distinguishes homomers from heteromers.
- **`sym_id`**: Symmetry operation identifier. For a homodimer with entity A, the two copies receive `sym_id` 1 and 2 respectively. For a heterodimer, both chains receive `sym_id` 1.
- **`asym_id`**: Unique chain identifier. Every chain gets a distinct `asym_id`, assigned sequentially.

The function groups chains by sequence, then constructs new dictionary keys of the form `{entity_letter}_{sym_id}` (e.g., `A_1`, `A_2` for a homodimer, `A_1`, `B_1` for a heterodimer). The `int_id_to_str_id()` helper encodes entity numbers in reverse-spreadsheet naming (1→A, 2→B, …, 27→AA), matching mmCIF conventions.

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L130-L167)

## The Core: Pair and Merge Pipeline

`feature_processing.pair_and_merge()` is the central function that transforms per-chain feature dictionaries into a single complex-level `FeatureDict`. It executes five sub-stages in strict order:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S1["process_unmerged_features()<br/>Deletion mean, atom mask,<br/>assembly_num_chains, entity_mask"] --> S2{"Is homomer<br/>or monomer?"}
    S2 -- "No (heteromer)" --> S3a["create_paired_features()<br/>Species-based MSA pairing"]
    S3a --> S3b["deduplicate_unpaired_sequences()<br/>Remove paired seqs from unpaired MSA"]
    S3b --> S4
    S2 -- "Yes" --> S4["crop_chains()<br/>MSA crop to 2048,<br/>templates to 4"]
    S4 --> S5["merge_chain_features()<br/>Block-diag MSA + concat paired"]
    S5 --> S6["process_final()<br/>Restype correction, masks,<br/>feature filtering"]

    style S3a fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
    style S5 fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#1e8e3e
```

### Stage 1: Unmerged Feature Processing

`process_unmerged_features()` operates on each chain independently before any cross-chain logic. It converts the integer deletion matrix to float32, computes `deletion_mean` (per-residue average deletion probability across the MSA), constructs `all_atom_mask` from the amino acid type using `STANDARD_ATOM_MASK`, initializes `all_atom_positions` to zeros (filled later by the structure module), sets `assembly_num_chains` to the total chain count, and computes `entity_mask` as `(entity_id != 0)`.

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L236-L272)

### Stage 2–3: MSA Pairing (Heteromers Only)

For heteromers, MSA pairing is the critical innovation. The goal is to construct **paired MSA rows** — alignments where sequences from different chains come from the **same species** and likely represent interacting partners in vivo. This is implemented in `msa_pairing.create_paired_features()`:

1. **`pair_sequences()`** — For each chain, `MSAStatistics.from_chain_features()` computes per-row species identifiers, sequence similarity to the target, and gap fraction. Chains are then grouped by species. For each species present in ≥2 chains, `_match_rows_by_sequence_similarity()` selects the top-k rows (by descending similarity) where k = min(count across chains). Species present in only one chain are **skipped entirely**, as they provide no pairing signal. Species with >600 sequences in any chain are also skipped (computational guardrail). The target sequences (row 0) are always paired first.

2. **`reorder_paired_rows()`** — Paired rows are ordered by: (a) number of chains in the pairing (all-chain pairings first), then (b) product of row indices (proxy for e-value ranking). This prioritizes the strongest evolutionary couplings.

3. **`pad_features()`** — Adds a padding row (gap sequence) at the end of each `_all_seq` feature. This pad row is selected when a chain lacks a paired sequence for a given species, ensuring rectangular arrays.

4. **`deduplicate_unpaired_sequences()`** — Removes any unpaired MSA rows that duplicate a sequence already present in the paired MSA, preventing redundant evolutionary information from inflating the MSA.

> [!TIP]
> MSA pairing is the primary mechanism by which AlphaFold-Multimer captures inter-chain evolutionary signal. Without it, the model would receive only block-diagonal MSAs with no cross-chain correlation — equivalent to predicting each chain independently. The UniProt database (unclustered) is essential because clustered databases like UniRef90 destroy the species-level pairing signal.

Sources: [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L70-L319), [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L74-L107)

### Stage 4: MSA Cropping

`crop_chains()` enforces memory and compute budgets by truncating each chain's MSA. The default `MSA_CROP_SIZE` is **2048** and `MAX_TEMPLATES` is **4**. For heteromers, the cropping strategy is nuanced: the paired MSA (`_all_seq` features) is cropped to at most `msa_crop_size // 2 = 1024` rows. The unpaired MSA crop size is then **reduced by the number of non-gapped paired rows**, keeping the total MSA size per chain roughly constant. This prevents paired sequences from inflating memory beyond the monomer budget. For homomers, simple truncation to `msa_crop_size` suffices since no pairing occurs.

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L110-L195)

### Stage 5: Chain Feature Merging

`merge_chain_features()` constructs the final unified feature dictionary through a carefully ordered sequence:

1. **`_pad_templates()`** — Pads each chain's template features to `max_templates` (4) rows with zeros, ensuring uniform template count.

2. **`_merge_homomers_dense_msa()`** — Groups chains by `entity_id` and merges identical chains by concatenating their MSA features along the residue dimension (`axis=1`), producing a **dense MSA** where homomeric copies share alignment rows. This is critical: a homodimer A₁A₂ should see the same MSA aligned to both copies, not a block-diagonal MSA with independent rows.

3. **`_merge_features_from_multiple_chains()`** — The central merge operation, applying different concatenation strategies per feature type:

| Feature Category | Merge Strategy | Axis | Rationale |
|-----------------|---------------|------|-----------|
| MSA features (unpaired) | Block-diagonal | `axis=1` (residues) | No evolutionary coupling between heteromer chains in unpaired MSA |
| MSA features (paired, `_all_seq`) | Concatenate | `axis=1` (residues) | Paired rows encode cross-chain evolutionary signal |
| Sequence features | Concatenate | `axis=0` (residues) | Chains are spatially sequential in the complex |
| Template features | Concatenate | `axis=1` (residues) | Template hits span the full complex |
| Chain features (`num_alignments`, `seq_length`) | Sum | — | Scalar accumulation across chains |

4. **`_concatenate_paired_and_unpaired_features()`** (heteromers only) — Stacks the paired MSA rows (`_all_seq`) **above** the block-diagonal unpaired rows along `axis=0`, producing the final MSA: `msa = concat([msa_all_seq, msa_block_diag], axis=0)`. The paired rows come first so the Evoformer processes the most informative cross-chain signals in the initial rows.

5. **`_correct_post_merged_feats()`** — Recomputes `seq_length`, `num_alignments`, and constructs `cluster_bias_mask` and `bert_mask`. For heteromers, `cluster_bias_mask` is 1 only for the first (target) row and 0 elsewhere. The `bert_mask` is constructed by concatenating the paired MSA mask (all 1s) with the block-diagonal unpaired MSA mask, ensuring the masked language model training signal respects the MSA structure.

> [!TIP]
> The block-diagonal MSA structure for unpaired rows is the default merging strategy when no cross-chain pairing is available (homomers/monomers). Off-diagonal blocks are filled with gap tokens and zero masks, effectively making the Evoformer's attention within those rows chain-local. Only the paired rows (prepended at the top) carry cross-chain information — this architectural choice keeps the memory footprint linear in chain count for unpaired regions.

Sources: [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L349-L543)

### Stage 6: Final Processing

`process_final()` applies four post-merge corrections: `_correct_msa_restypes()` remaps MSA residue types from HHblits ordering to AlphaFold's internal ordering via `MAP_HHBLITS_AATYPE_TO_OUR_AATYPE`; `_make_seq_mask()` creates `seq_mask = (entity_id > 0)`; `_make_msa_mask()` creates `msa_mask` as all-ones masked by `seq_mask`; and `_filter_features()` retains only the 24 features listed in `REQUIRED_FEATURES`, discarding intermediate keys like `msa_all_seq` and `deletion_matrix_int`.

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L24-L57), [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L198-L233)

## MSA Padding and Output

After `pair_and_merge()` returns, `pad_msa()` ensures the MSA has at least **512** sequences. If the merged MSA has fewer rows, it zero-pads `msa`, `deletion_matrix`, `bert_mask`, `msa_mask`, and `cluster_bias_mask` along the sequence dimension. This prevents the `extra_msa` subset (created during TF input pipeline processing) from being zero-sized, which would cause shape errors in the model.

The final output is a single `FeatureDict` with keys spanning the full complex — all chains' residues concatenated — ready for `model.RunModel.process_features()` and subsequent neural network inference.

Sources: [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L170-L181), [pipeline_multimer.py](/alphafold/data/pipeline_multimer.py#L269-L320)

## Homomer vs. Heteromer: Feature Assembly Decision Tree

The pipeline dynamically adapts its behavior based on the input complex type, which is determined by `_is_homomer_or_monomer()` checking whether `num_unique_chains == 1`:

| Aspect | Homomer / Monomer | Heteromer |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|
| UniProt `_all_seq` MSA | Not generated | Generated via jackhmmer against UniProt |
| MSA pairing | Skipped | Species-based `create_paired_features()` |
| Deduplication | Skipped | `deduplicate_unpaired_sequences()` |
| Unpaired MSA merge | Block-diagonal | Block-diagonal |
| Paired MSA merge | N/A | Concatenated above unpaired |
| Homomer dense MSA | Chains merged by entity_id | Chains merged by entity_id |
| `cluster_bias_mask` | 1 for first row of each block | 1 for row 0 only |
| `bert_mask` | Block-diagonal only | Paired mask ⊕ block-diagonal mask |

For a homodimer A₁A₂, the pipeline merges both copies into a single dense MSA block — the same evolutionary alignment applies to both chains since they share identical sequence. For a heterodimer AB, the MSA has a paired block on top (species-matched rows across both chains) followed by a block-diagonal unpaired block (A's MSA and B's MSA as independent blocks).

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L60-L107), [msa_pairing.py](/alphafold/data/msa_pairing.py#L358-L408)

## Required Feature Set

The multimer pipeline's `REQUIRED_FEATURES` frozenset defines the 24 features that survive the final filtering step. These are the precise inputs the multimer neural network expects:

```
aatype, all_atom_mask, all_atom_positions, all_chains_entity_ids,
all_crops_all_chains_mask, all_crops_all_chains_positions,
all_crops_all_chains_residue_ids, assembly_num_chains, asym_id,
bert_mask, cluster_bias_mask, deletion_matrix, deletion_mean,
entity_id, entity_mask, mem_peak, msa, msa_mask, num_alignments,
num_templates, queue_size, residue_index, resolution, seq_length,
seq_mask, sym_id, template_aatype, template_all_atom_mask,
template_all_atom_positions
```

Note the three multimer-specific features absent from the monomer pipeline: **`asym_id`**, **`entity_id`**, and **`sym_id`** — the assembly annotation triple that enables the model to distinguish chain identity, sequence equivalence, and symmetry relationships.

Sources: [feature_processing.py](/alphafold/data/feature_processing.py#L24-L57)

## Navigation

The multimer feature assembly feeds directly into the neural network. To understand how these assembled features are consumed:

- **[Evoformer and Embeddings](11-evoformer-and-embeddings)** — How the paired MSA and assembly IDs initialize the Evoformer's attention patterns
- **[Invariant Point Attention](12-invariant-point-attention)** — The geometric attention mechanism that leverages `asym_id` for chain-aware structural reasoning
- **[MSA Generation Workflow](8-msa-generation-workflow)** — The monomer MSA generation that underpins per-chain features before multimer assembly

# Evoformer and Embeddings



The **Evoformer** is the computational heart of AlphaFold — a deep transformer-like architecture that jointly evolves an MSA representation and a pairwise representation across 48 iterative blocks. Before the Evoformer stack runs, an **embedding phase** converts raw input features (amino acid sequences, MSAs, templates, and positional encodings) into dense tensor representations. Together, `EmbeddingsAndEvoformer` forms the single most critical module in the neural network core, consuming the majority of inference time and producing the representations that feed every downstream head.

## The EmbeddingsAndEvoformer Module

The `AlphaFoldIteration` class instantiates `EmbeddingsAndEvoformer` as its first and most substantial sub-module, directly consuming the input batch to produce a dictionary of representations. The class bridges two conceptually distinct phases — **input embedding** (converting sparse biological signals into dense vectors) and **Evoformer iteration** (co-evolving MSA and pair representations through shared-attention blocks).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph EmbeddingsAndEvoformer
        direction TB
        Input[Input Batch] --> Emb[Embedding Phase]
        Emb --> MSA_Emb[MSA Representation<br/>N_seq × N_res × 256]
        Emb --> Pair_Emb[Pair Representation<br/>N_res × N_res × 128]
        
        MSA_Emb --> Evo[Evoformer Stack<br/>×48 blocks]
        Pair_Emb --> Evo
        
        Evo --> MSA_Out[Final MSA Rep<br/>N_seq × N_res × 256]
        Evo --> Pair_Out[Final Pair Rep<br/>N_res × N_res × 128]
        
        MSA_Out --> Single[Single Representation<br/>N_res × 384]
        Pair_Out --> Pair_Final[Pair Representation<br/>N_res × N_res × 128]
    end
    
    Single --> Heads[Downstream Heads]
    Pair_Final --> Heads
```

Within `AlphaFoldIteration.__call__`, the module is constructed and invoked at the start of every recycling iteration. The returned representations dictionary contains three primary tensors: **`msa`** (the full MSA representation, not ensembled), **`pair`** (the pairwise representation, ensembled across input crops), and **`single`** (a per-residue representation derived from the first row of the MSA, used by the structure module). When ensembling is active, the pair and single representations are averaged across ensemble members while the MSA representation from the first crop is retained.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L134-L211), [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L289-L411)

## Embedding Phase: From Biological Signals to Dense Vectors

The embedding phase converts heterogeneous input features into the two core tensor representations that the Evoformer will evolve. This is where raw discrete signals — amino acid types, MSA rows, residue indices, and optionally template structures — become continuous vectors in learned embedding spaces.

### Target Feature Embedding

The target (query) sequence is encoded as a one-hot vector over 20 standard amino acids plus an unknown token, yielding a **`target_feat`** of shape `[N_res, 21]`. This serves as the basis for the single representation and is linearly projected into the MSA channel space (c_m = 256) to initialize the first row of the MSA representation — the row corresponding to the query sequence itself.

### MSA Feature Embedding

The MSA input features (`msa_feat`) are a pre-computed tensor of shape `[N_seq, N_res, 49]` containing: a 23-dimensional one-hot encoding of each MSA residue (20 amino acids + unknown + gap + BERT mask), a binary deletion indicator, and a deletion value feature. This tensor is linearly projected from 49 input channels into the MSA channel dimension c_m = 256. The query sequence's target feature embedding is added to the first row, anchoring the MSA representation to the true sequence.

### Pair Feature Embedding

The pair representation is initialized from **relative positional encodings**. The residue index difference `residue_index[i] - residue_index[j]` is clipped to the range `[-max_relative_feature, max_relative_feature]` (default ±32) and one-hot encoded into 65 bins. This 65-dimensional vector is linearly projected into the pair channel dimension c_z = 128. This encoding captures the sequential distance between residues — a critical structural prior since sequentially adjacent residues are also spatially proximate in folded proteins.

### Recycling Embeddings

When recycling is enabled (the default), previous iteration outputs are injected into the embeddings. Three recycling signals are supported: **`prev_msa_first_row`** (added to the first M%MSA row), **`prev_pair`** ("added to the pair representation), and **`prev_pos`** (converted to a distogram and embedded into the pair). The positional distogram bins 15 distance ranges from 3.25Å to 20.75Å, providing spatial priors from the previous structure prediction.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L364-L376), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L239-L377)

## Channel Dimensions and Architecture Constants

The embedding and Evoformer architecture is governed by four primary channel dimensions that control the representational capacity at each stage:

| Channel | Symbol | Dimension | Tensor Shape | Purpose |
|---------|--------|-----------|--------------|---------|
| `msa_channel` | c_m | 256 | `[N_seq, N_res, 256]` | MSA representation per residue per sequence |
| `pair_channel` | c_z | 128 | `[N_res, N_res, 128]` | Pairwise relationship between residue pairs |
| `seq_channel` | c_s | 384 | `[N_res, 384]` | Single (per-residue) representation for structure module |
| `extra_msa_channel` | c_e | 64 | `[N_extra, N_res, 64]` | Extra MSA stack (lower capacity) |

The single representation (c_s = 384) is derived from the first MSA row via a linear projection from c_m = 256 to c_s = 384, effectively expanding the representational bandwidth for the structure module. The asymmetry between c_m and c_s reflects the different demands of MSA co-evolution reasoning versus 3D coordinate construction.

Sources: [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L307-L315)

## The Evoformer Block: Joint MSA–Pair Evolution

Each of the 48 Evoformer blocks applies a fixed sequence of operations that alternate between updating the MSA representation and the pair representation, with information flowing bidirectionally between them. This joint evolution is the key architectural innovation — the MSA rows communicate structural hypotheses to the pair representation, while the pair representation biases attention patterns in the MSA rows.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph EvoformerBlock["Evoformer Block (×48)"]
        direction TB
        MSA_in["MSA Rep<br/>N_seq × N_res × c_m"] --> MSA_Row_Attn
        Pair_in["Pair Rep<br/>N_res × N_res × c_z"] --> MSA_Row_Attn
        
        MSA_Row_Attn["1. MSA Row Attention<br/>with Pair Bias"] --> MSA_Col_Attn
        MSA_Col_Attn["2. MSA Column Attention<br/>(Global for extra)"] --> MSA_Trans
        MSA_Trans["3. MSA Transition<br/>(2-layer MLP)"] --> OPM
        MSA_Trans --> OPM
        OPM["4. Outer Product Mean<br/>(MSA → Pair)"] --> TriMult_Out
        
        Pair_in --> TriMult_Out
        TriMult_Out["5. Triangle Multiplication<br/>Outgoing"] --> TriMult_In
        TriMult_In["6. Triangle Multiplication<br/>Incoming"] --> TriAttn_Start
        TriAttn_Start["7. Triangle Attention<br/>Starting Node"] --> TriAttn_End
        TriAttn_End["8. Triangle Attention<br/>Ending Node"] --> Pair_Trans
        Pair_Trans["9. Pair Transition<br/>(2-layer MLP)"]
        
        MSA_Trans --> MSA_out["MSA Rep (updated)"]
        Pair_Trans --> Pair_out["Pair Rep (updated)"]
    end
```

Every sub-operation follows a **residual + dropout** pattern enforced by `dropout_wrapper`, which applies the sub-module, optionally drops elements, and adds the result back to the input activation. This ensures stable gradient flow across all 48 blocks.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L66-L105), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L240-L306)

### MSA Row Attention with Pair Bias

This is the mechanism by which the pair representation directly influences MSA reasoning. For each MSA sequence row, standard multi-head attention operates across the residue dimension. The critical addition is a **pair bias term**: the pair representation is LayerNorm'd, then linearly projected from c_z = 128 to `num_head` = 8 bias values, producing a nonbatched bias of shape `[H, N_res, N_res]` added to the attention logits before softmax.

This means the attention pattern for each MSA row "knows" which residue pairs the pair representation currently believes are structurally coupled — even though the MSA itself contains no explicit spatial information. The pair bias creates an inductive loop: structural hypotheses in the pair representation guide where the MSA attends, and the resulting MSA updates flow back to the pair representation via the Outer Product Mean.

The attention uses 8 heads with gating (sigmoid-gated output), per-row shared dropout (broadcast along the sequence dimension), and a dropout rate of 0.15 during training.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L795-L855), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L242-L248)

### MSA Column Attention

Column attention transposes the MSA representation so that attention operates **across MSA sequences** at each residue position. This allows each residue to attend to the distribution of amino acids across evolutionary homologs7 — capturing conservation patterns, co-evolution signals, and positional entropy. The implementation swaps axes `-2` and `-3` before and after applying standard `Attention` with 8 heads, gating, and no dropout (rate = 0.0).

For the **extra MSA stack** (4 blocks operating on the larger extra MSA), a `MSAColumnGlobalAttention` variant is used instead. Global attention computes a single query vector per column by averaging across valid sequences, then broadcasts the attention output — a significant memory optimization when N_extra_seq ≫ N_seq.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L858-L960), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L249:9-L255)

### MSA Transition

A two-layer MLP (Linear → ReLU → Linear) applied independently to each position in the MSA representation, with anA intermediate factor of 4× (expanding from 256 → 1024 → 256). The transition is applied per-row with `LayerNorm` on input and shared dropout. This provides the feed-forward component familiar from transformer architectures.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L515-L570), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L256-L261)

### Outer Product Mean: MSA → Pair Communication

The `OuterProductMean` is the primary channel through which MSA information flows into the pair representation. For each MSA sequence, the representationC is projected into left and right vectors of dimension `num_outer_channel` = 32. The outer product `left[s,i,c-] ⊗ right[s,j,c']` is computed for each sequence and pair (i, j), then averaged across sequences (normalized by the number of valid sequence pairs at each position). The result is contracted with a learned weight tensor and projected to c_z = 128.

This operation is mathematically rich: the outer product captures **second-order correlations** between residue positions across the MSA. When positions i and j co-vary across homologs (a hallmark of physical contact), the outer products constructively interfere, strengthening the corresponding pair representation entry. The chunked computation (chunk_size = 128) and subbatching manage memory for the large `[N_res, N_res, c_z]` output tensor.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L1600-L1689), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L262-L269)

### Triangle Multiplication and Triangle Attention

These four operations form the **geometric reasoning core** of the pair stack, operating on the triangular structure of the `[N_res, N_res, c_z]` pair tensor. They are the most computationally expensive components and embody the principle that if residues i and k interact, and residues k and j interact, then residues i and j likely interact too — a transitivity constraint on structural contacts.

**Triangle Multiplication** comes in two orientations defined by Einstein summation equations:
- **Outgoing**: `ikc,jkc→ijc` — for each edge (i,j), combines all edges sharing a starting node i
- **Incoming**: `kjc,kic→ijc` — for each edge (i,j), combines all edges sharing an ending node j

Each projects the pair representation to left and right intermediate channels (128), computes the element-wise product along the shared index k, then projects back to c_z. Gating with a sigmoid is applied. The `fuse_projection_weights` flag (default `False` in v3) controls whether the left/right projections share weights — a numerical optimization trade-off.

**Triangle Attention** also comes in two orientations:
- **Starting node** (`per_row`): attends along rows of the pair tensor, with bias from the pair itself
- **Ending node**0 (`per_column`): attends along columns, with analogous bias

Both use 4 attention heads with gating and dropout rate of 0.25. The self-bias mechanism (projecting pair features to head(6dimensional biases) is identical to the pair bias in MSA row attention, creating a consistent architectural pattern.

| Operation | Eq. | Heads | Intermediate Ch. | Dropout |
|-----------|-----|-------|-------------------|---------|
| Triangle Mult. Outgoing | `ikc,jkc→ijc` | — | 128 | 0.25 |
| Triangle Mult. Incoming | `kjc,kic→ijc` | — | 128 | 0.25 |
| Triangle Attn. Starting | per_row | 4 | — | 0.25 |
| Triangle Attn. Ending | per_column | 4 | — | 0.25 |

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L963-L1024), [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L1400-L1516), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L270-L305)

### Pair Transition

Identical in structure to MSA Transition: a two-layer MLP (128 → 512 → 128) with LayerNorm, applied per-row with shared dropout. The intermediate factor is 4× and dropout rate is 0.0.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L515-L570), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L300-L305)

## Extra MSA Stack

Before the main Evoformer runs, a smaller **Extra MSA Stack** processes the larger pool of MSA sequences that weren't selected as cluster centers. This stack uses only 4 blocks (vs. 48 for the main Evoformer) and operates at reduced channel capacity (c_e = 64 vs. c_m = 256). Its purpose is to extract additional evolutionary signal from the ~10K extra MSA sequences and inject it into the pair representation.

The extra MSA feature tensor is constructed by `create_extra_msa_feature`, which concatenates: a 23-dimensional one-hot encoding of each extra MSA residue, a binary deletion indicator, and a deletion count value — yielding 25 input channels projected to c_e = 64. Each block of the extra stack contains MSA row attention with pair bias, MSA column global attention, MSA transition, outer product mean, and the full pair stack (triangle multiplication + triangle attention + pair transition).

> [!TIP]
> The extra MSA stack's pair operations share the same pair representation as the main Evoformer — it is **not** a separate pair tensor. This means the extra stack "pre-conditions" the pair representation with additional evolutionary signal before the main Evoformer even begins, providing a richer starting point for the 48-block evolution.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L108-L131), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L307-L309)

## Template Embedding

When templates are enabled (models 1 and 2), template structures are embedded into the pair representation before the Evoformer runs. Each template's pairwise distance histogram (distogram) is computed from pseudo-beta positions and one-hot encoded over 39 distance bins (3.25Å to: 50.75Å). Template backbone torsion angles may also be embedded (for models 1.1.x). These template features pass through a `TemplatePairStack` (2 blocks of triangle attention and multiplication) and are aggregated across templates via attention weighted by the template's `sum_probs` score. The resulting template pair representation is added to the main pair representation, seeding it with structural priors from known homologs.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L414-L512), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L316-L376)

## Dropout and Training Considerations

The Evoformer employs a carefully differentiated dropout strategy. **MSA row attention** uses the highest dropout (0.15) since it is the primary information bottleneck. **Triangle operations** use 0.25 dropout — high because the triangle multiplications are the most parameter-intensive components and most prone to overfitting. **Transition layers and column attention** use zero dropout, as they serve as deterministic transformations. All dropout uses **shared (broadcast) dropout** along the orientationD spatial dimension, meaning the same dropout mask is applied to all residues or pairs — a form of spatial regularization that prevents the model from memorizing position-specific patterns.

The `dropout_wrapper` function enforces a residual connection pattern: `output = input_act + dropout(module(input_act))`. During evaluation, dropout is disabled unless `eval_dropout` is explicitly set in the global config.

Sources: [modules.py](alphafold/model/modules.py#L52-L105), [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L378-L385)

## Model Variant Differences

The five AlphaFold model variants differ primarily in their embedding=and Evoformer configuration:

| Variant | Templates | Extra MSA | Torsion Embed | pAE Head | Evoformer Blocks |
|---------|-----------|-----------|---------------|----------|-----------------|
| model_1 | ✓ | 5120 | ✓ | ✗ | 48 |
| model_2 | ✓ | 1024 | ✓ | ✗ | 48 |
| model_3 | ✗ | 5120 | ✗ | ✗ | 48 |
| model_4 | ✗ | 5120 | ✗ | ✗ | 48 |
| model_5 | ✗ | 1024 | ✗ | ✗ | 48 |

The ptm variants add a `predicted_aligned_error` head (weight 0.1) atop the corresponding base model. Multimer variants (v3) adjust `num_msa` to 252, `num_extra_m0sa` to 1152, and disable weight fusion in triangle multiplication for numerical optimization.

Sources: [config.py](alphafold/model/config.py#L55-L134)

```mermaid

    end
```

> [!TIP]
> The Evoformer's architectural power stems from **bidirectional information flow**: the Outer Product Mean carries MSA co-evolution signals into the pair representation (bottom-up), while the Pair Bias in MSA Row Attention carries structural hypotheses back into MSA reasoning (top-down). This feedback loop, repeated 48 times, enables the model to iteratively refine which evolutionary patterns are structurally meaningful and which spatial constraints are evolutionarily supported.

## Where to Go Next

The Evoformer's pair representation feeds directly into [Invariant Point Attention](12-invariant-point-attention), which operates on the single representation while conditioned on the pair. The final MSA and pair representations also drive [Structure Module and Folding](13-structure-module-and-folding), and the recycling mechanism in [Recycling Mechanism](14-recycling-mechanism) feeds predictions back into the embedding phase described above. For the geometric primitives underlying the triangle operations, see [Quaternion Affine Transforms](15-quaternion-affine-transforms).

# Invariant Point Attention



Invariant Point Attention (IPA) is the geometric reasoning engine at the heart of AlphaFold's Structure Module — a multi-head attention mechanism that operates natively over 3D points and orientations, guaranteeing **SE(3)-equivariance** by construction rather than by enforcement. Unlike standard attention that reasons over abstract vector spaces, IPA anchors every query, key, and value to physical coordinates in space, making the attention weights invariant to global rotations and translations while the output transforms equivariantly. This design is what enables AlphaFold to refine backbone geometry iteratively without ever breaking the spatial coherence of the predicted structure.

Sources: [folding.py](/alphafold/model/folding.py#L37-L48)

## Mathematical Foundation

The central insight behind IPA is that **Euclidean distance is invariant to rigid-body transformations**. If two points are expressed in their own local reference frames, transforming them into a shared global frame and computing their distance yields the same result regardless of what that global frame is. IPA exploits this by having each residue produce query and key *points* in its local frame, projecting them to the global frame via the current backbone affine, and then computing attention logits from the squared pairwise distances between these global-frame points.

The complete attention logit for head $h$, query residue $i$, and key residue $j$ is:

$$\text{logit}_{hij} = w_s \cdot \mathbf{q}^s_{hi} \cdot \mathbf{k}^s_{hj} \;-\; \frac{w_p}{2} \sum_{d \in \{x,y,z\}} \left( q^p_{hid} - k^p_{hjd} \right)^2 \;+\; w_a \cdot b_{hij}$$

where $\mathbf{q}^s, \mathbf{k}^s$ are scalar queries/keys, $q^p, k^p$ are point queries/keys in the global frame, $b_{hij}$ is a 2D bias projected from the pair representation, and $w_s, w_p, w_a$ are variance-normalizing weights that balance the three logit terms. The negative squared distance term means that residues with nearby 3D query/key points produce higher attention scores — the module naturally focuses on spatial neighbors.

> [!TIP]
> Unlike naive approaches that would enforce equivariance via regularization or data augmentation, IPA achieves it **architecturally**: the only geometric operation is point projection through learned affines and Euclidean distance computation, both of which are inherently SE(3)-compatible. No symmetry-breaking can occur.

Sources: [folding.py](/alphafold/model/folding.py#L168-L212)

## Architecture and Data Flow

The following diagram illustrates the complete data flow through the IPA module, from raw embeddings to the final output projection:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs
        I1D["inputs_1d<br/>(N, C)"]
        I2D["inputs_2d<br/>(N, N, C')"]
        MSK["mask<br/>(N, 1)"]
        AFF["QuatAffine<br/>(rotation + translation)"]
    end

    subgraph Scalar_Projections["Scalar Projections"]
        QS["q_scalar<br/>Linear → reshape<br/>(N, H, c_qk)"]
        KVS["kv_scalar<br/>Linear → reshape + split"]
        KS["k_scalar<br/>(N, H, c_qk)"]
        VS["v_scalar<br/>(N, H, c_v)"]
        KVS --> KS & VS
    end

    subgraph Point_Projections["Point Projections (Local → Global)"]
        QPL["q_point_local<br/>Linear → split by xyz"]
        KVL["kv_point_local<br/>Linear → split by xyz"]
        QPG["q_point_global<br/>affine.apply_to_point"]
        KVG["kv_point_global<br/>affine.apply_to_point"]
        QPL -->|"project to<br/>global frame"| QPG
        KVL -->|"project to<br/>global frame"| KVG
    end

    subgraph Logit_Computation["Logit Computation"]
        SL["scalar_logits<br/>w_s · q · k^T"]
        PL["point_logits<br/>-0.5 · w_p · ||q - k||²"]
        BL["2d_bias<br/>w_a · Linear(inputs_2d)"]
        LOGITS["attn_logits = SL + PL + BL"]
        SL & PL & BL --> LOGITS
    end

    subgraph Weighted_Aggregation["Weighted Aggregation"]
        SM["softmax(logits)"]
        RS["result_scalar<br/>attn · v_scalar"]
        RP["result_point_global<br/>attn · v_point"]
        RA2D["result_attn_over_2d<br/>attn · inputs_2d"]
    end

    subgraph Output_Assembly["Output Assembly"]
        RPL["result_point_local<br/>affine.invert_point"]
        DN["point_distance_norm<br/>√(ε + x² + y² + z²)"]
        CAT["concat all features"]
        OUT["Linear → (N, num_channel)"]
    end

    I1D --> QS & KVS & QPL & KVL
    I2D --> BL & RA2D
    AFF --> QPG & KVG & RPL
    QPG --> PL
    KVG --> PL & RP
    QS --> SL
    KS --> SL
    VS --> RS
    LOGITS --> SM
    SM --> RS & RP & RA2D
    RP --> RPL
```
